subtitle: Definition R = (1/M) sum m_i r_i; standard bodies table; symmetry; discrete and continuous drills.
takeaway: R = (1/M) sum m_i r_i: the mass-weighted average position; symmetry pins it, holes shift it.

cards.title: The centre of mass: the mass-weighted average position
items: For $n$ particles the centre of mass (COM) is $\mathbf{R} = \dfrac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i \mathbf{r}_i$ with $M = \sum m_i$. Component form: $X_{cm} = \sum m_i x_i / M$, $Y_{cm} = \sum m_i y_i / M$.

For a continuous body $\mathbf{R} = \frac{1}{M}\int \mathbf{r}\,dm$, integrated over the body with $dm = \rho\,dV$ (or $\lambda\,dl$, $\sigma\,dA$ for line/surface mass). The COM is unique, independent of the coordinate origin (shift both sides of the definition and $\mathbf{R}$ shifts with them), and transforms like a position vector. Always pick the origin so that symmetry kills one or both integrals before integrating.

cards.title: The centre of mass: the mass-weighted average position (cont.)
items: Worked habits: place the origin ON a symmetry axis; use the standard-bodies table below as building blocks; cut composite bodies into pieces with known COMs and average those. For a body with a hole, the fastest route is negative mass (CM-02).
the COM is the one point whose motion answers to external forces alone - it is the reduction of a complicated system to one particle for the purpose of the momentum ledger (CM-03).

cards.title: Physical meaning and symmetry shortcuts
items: Physical meaning: $\mathbf{R}$ is the point whose motion answers to external forces alone (CM-03). For any system at all - a gas cloud, a gymnast mid-flight, an exploded shell - the mass-weighted mean position is the one point whose trajectory is simple. The COM may lie in empty space: for a uniform ring it is at the centre, for a boomerang it may be off the body entirely. Nothing requires mass to exist at the COM. Symmetry shortcuts:

cards.title: Physical meaning and symmetry shortcuts (cont.)
items: an axis of symmetry forces the COM onto that axis; two symmetry axes force it to their intersection; a plane of symmetry forces it into that plane. A uniform body with a centre of symmetry has its COM at that centre.

Discrete systems: $X_{cm} = (m_1x_1 + m_2x_2 + \cdots)/M$. Two masses $m_1, m_2$ at separation $d$: the COM divides the line joining them in the RATIO $m_2 : m_1$ - it sits closer to the heavier mass. Composite bodies: cut into pieces with known COMs and average.

title: The centre of mass: the mass-weighted average position (cont.)
subtitle: Definition R = (1/M) sum m_i r_i; standard bodies table; symmetry; discrete and continuous drills.
takeaway: R = (1/M) sum m_i r_i: the mass-weighted average position; symmetry pins it, holes shift it.

cards.title: Physical meaning and symmetry shortcuts (cont.)
items: Trap: the COM of a body is NOT necessarily inside it; and it is not the geometric centre unless the body is uniform AND symmetric. A ring with a bead glued on has its COM pulled toward the bead; shift to the negative-mass picture the moment a cut appears (CM-02).

centroid by vertices: triangle $(0,0), (b,0), (0,h)$ has centroid $(b/3, h/3)$; the distance from the base is $h/3$ and from the $x = 0$ side it is $b/3$ - the medians rule. Four equal masses at the corners of a square give the square centre.

cards.title: Standard shapes table (memorise; two-line integrals)
items: Standard results (memorise; each is a two-line integral to re-derive): uniform rod length $L$: midpoint, $L/2$ from either end. Uniform triangle: the centroid, intersection of the medians, at distance $h/3$ from any side (i.e. one-third of the altitude from each base). Semicircular ring of radius $R$: $y_{cm} = 2R/\pi \approx 0.637R$ from the diameter. Semicircular disc:

$y_{cm} = 4R/(3\pi) \approx 0.424R$ from the diameter. Solid hemisphere: $3R/8 = 0.375R$ from the flat face. Hollow hemisphere (shell): $R/2$ from the flat face. Solid cone of height $h$: $h/4$ from the base (i.e. $3h/4$ from the apex). Uniform circular arc subtending angle $\theta$ at the centre: $x_{cm} = R\sin(\theta/2)/(\theta/2)$ from the centre along the bisector.

cards.title: Standard shapes table (memorise; two-line integrals)
items: Line distributions: uniform rod on the $x$-axis from $0$ to $L$: $dm = (M/L)dx$, $X_{cm} = \frac{1}{M}\int_0^L \frac{M}{L}x\,dx = L/2$. Semicircular ring by angle: $dm = (M/\pi)d\phi$, $y = R\sin\phi$: $y_{cm} = \frac{1}{M}\int_0^\pi \frac{M}{\pi}R\sin\phi\,d\phi = \frac{2R}{\pi}$. Semicircular disc by shells:
$dm = (2M/R^2) r\,dr$ half-rings, each at $y = 2r/\pi$: integrate to $4R/(3\pi)$.
the table values are the standard-exam vocabulary: every composite COM problem reduces to these blocks plus the weighted average.

cards.title: Why the table values sit where they do
items: WHY the ring beats the disc ($2/\pi > 4/(3\pi)$) because the ring puts all its mass at radius $R$, so the average height above the diameter is larger than for the disc where interior mass pulls the average down. The shell hemisphere ($R/2$) sits higher than the solid one ($3R/8$) for the same reason. The cone's $h/4$ reflects the $r^2$ mass weighting toward the base.

CHECK sanity of every table entry: all distances are positive, less than the body size, and shrink correctly with the body. Arc limit: as $\theta \to 0$, $\sin(\theta/2)/(\theta/2) \to 1$ and the arc becomes a point mass at radius $R$; as $\theta \to \pi$ the arc becomes a semicircular ring and $R\sin(\pi/2)/(\pi/2) = 2R/\pi$ exactly matches the table.

title: The centre of mass: the mass-weighted average position (cont.)
subtitle: Definition R = (1/M) sum m_i r_i; standard bodies table; symmetry; discrete and continuous drills.
takeaway: R = (1/M) sum m_i r_i: the mass-weighted average position; symmetry pins it, holes shift it.

cards.title: Why the table values sit where they do (cont.)
items: self-audit before any exam submit: units (length), symmetry argument stated, and the result moves the right way when a mass grows.

To find the COM of a body with a hole, SUPERPOSE: treat the holed body as the full solid body PLUS a negative-mass piece filling the hole. $M\mathbf{R} = M_1\mathbf{r}_1 - M_2\mathbf{r}_2$ so $\mathbf{R} = \dfrac{M_1\mathbf{r}_1 - M_2\mathbf{r}_2}{M_1 - M_2}$, with $M_2$ the mass the removed material would have had. The result is algebraically identical to integrating the remaining body, and far faster.

cards.title: The negative-mass trick: cutting a hole (cont.)
items: Classic (source E1-family): uniform disc of radius $R$, mass $M_1$; a hole of radius $R/2$ is cut with its centre at $R/2$ from the disc centre. Densities match, so $M_2 = M_1/4$ (mass scales with area). Set the disc centre at the origin and the hole centre at $R/2$: $X = \frac{M_1(0) - (M_1/4)(R/2)}{M_1 - M_1/4} = \frac{-M_1R/8}{3M_1/4} = -\frac{R}{6}$.
The COM sits on the OPPOSITE side of the disc centre, at $R/6$ - it never lies inside the hole; it shifts AWAY from the cut.

cards.title: The negative-mass trick: cutting a hole (cont.)
items: General recipe: (1) choose an origin at a symmetry point of the FULL body; (2) compute $M_2$ from area/volume ratios; (3) plug into the formula with the SIGNED mass; (4) sanity-check the direction: the COM always moves away from the removed material. Equivalent viewpoint: keep the hole positive and subtract - the superposition is exact because the mass distribution is additive.

the trick works because $\int_{body\setminus hole} = \int_{body} - \int_{hole}$ linearity: mass, first moments, and the COM definition are all linear in the mass distribution. It is the same reason superposition works for fields.

cards.title: The negative-mass trick: cutting a hole (cont.)
items: limits: $M_2 \to 0$ gives $R \to \mathbf{r}_1$ (no cut, no shift); $M_2 \to M_1$ (cut everything) gives a vanishing denominator - the formula correctly refuses. For the $R/2$-hole disc, shift $R/6$ is less than $R/2$ ok between centre and hole edge; check by symmetry that the COM stays on the centre-hole line.

E1-style worked numbers (source E1): a plate made of two pieces: piece A mass 2 kg with COM at (1, 2) cm, piece B mass 3 kg with COM at (3, 1) cm: $X = (2(1) + 3(3))/5 = 11/5 = 2.2$ cm; $Y = (2(2) + 3(1))/5 = 7/5 = 1.4$ cm. Source E1 prints 2.21 and 1.07 for its own geometry - the method is identical: weighted average of piece COMs.

title: The negative-mass trick: cutting a hole is adding a negative piece
subtitle: Negative-mass hole trick, composite averaging, origin invariance, drills.
takeaway: Treat a hole as negative mass: R = (M1 r1 - M2 r2)/(M1 - M2); the COM always shifts away from the cut.

cards.title: Composite bodies: cut, place, average (cont.)
items: L-shape from three identical squares of side $a$: place the corner at the origin; square COMs at $(a/2, a/2)$, $(3a/2, a/2)$, $(a/2, 3a/2)$: $X_{cm} = (0.5a + 1.5a + 0.5a)/3 = 5a/6$ and $Y_{cm} = (0.5a + 0.5a + 1.5a)/3 = 5a/6$. The COM sits at $(5a/6, 5a/6)$ from the outer corner, on the diagonal symmetry line.

Composite discipline: never integrate what you can look up. The exam plate problems are always two standard shapes glued or one shape cut; the negative-mass trick handles cuts, the weighted average handles gluing.

cards.title: Composite bodies: cut, place, average (cont.)
items: L-tromino sanity: the COM must lie on the diagonal symmetry line $x = y$ ok ($5a/6 = 5a/6$); and inside the bounding square ok.

(a) Uniform rod of length $L$ with the left third removed: full rod COM $L/2$; removed piece mass $M/3$ at $L/6$: $X = \frac{M(L/2) - (M/3)(L/6)}{2M/3} = \frac{L/2 - L/18}{2/3} = \frac{8L/18}{2/3} = \frac{2L}{3}$. The remaining two-thirds has its COM at $2L/3$ from the left end ok (uniform rod from $L/3$ to $L$ has midpoint $2L/3$ ok).

cards.title: Drills: holes, plates, and three-mass systems (cont.)
items: (b) Disc radius $R$ with a concentric hole of radius $R/2$: $X = 0$ by symmetry (the negative-mass formula gives $0/3M/4 = 0$ ok). (c) Three masses 1, 2, 3 kg at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side 2 m: $X = (1(0) + 2(2) + 3(1))/6 = 7/6$ m; $Y = (0 + 0 + 3\sqrt{3})/6 = \sqrt{3}/2$ m... with vertices $(0,0), (2,0), (1,\sqrt{3})$ ok.
drill (a) is the composite standard check: a uniform rod's COM is its midpoint whatever the slice ok; drill (c) sits inside the triangle's bounding box ok and is pulled toward the 3 kg corner ok.

cards.title: Shift the origin: the invariance habit
items: The COM formula is origin-independent in the right way: shift all coordinates by $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ shifts by $\mathbf{a}$; the PHYSICAL answer (the location of the COM in the body) is unchanged. Exam habit: set the origin at the largest symmetry point; compute; translate only if the question asked for a specific frame.

Two-mass shortcut: $\mathbf{R} = \frac{m_1\mathbf{r}_1 + m_2\mathbf{r}_2}{m_1+m_2}$ can always be written $\mathbf{r}_1 + \frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}(\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1)$: the COM lies a fraction $\frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}$ of the way from mass 1 to mass 2. This single sentence answers most discrete-COM geometry questions.

title: The negative-mass trick: cutting a hole is adding a negative piece (cont.)
subtitle: Negative-mass hole trick, composite averaging, origin invariance, drills.
takeaway: Treat a hole as negative mass: R = (M1 r1 - M2 r2)/(M1 - M2); the COM always shifts away from the cut.

cards.title: Shift the origin: the invariance habit (cont.)
items: the fraction form: for equal masses it gives the midpoint ok; for $m_2 \to 0$ the COM stays at $\mathbf{r}_1$ ok; for $m_1 \to 0$ it goes to $\mathbf{r}_2$ ok.

Newton's second law for a SYSTEM: $M\mathbf{a}_{cm} = \mathbf{F}_{ext}$ - internal forces cancel in third-law pairs and can never accelerate the COM. Proof in one line: $M\ddot{\mathbf{R}} = \sum m_i\ddot{\mathbf{r}}_i = \sum \mathbf{F}_i = \sum \mathbf{F}_i^{ext} + \sum_{pairs}(\mathbf{f}_{ij}+\mathbf{f}_{ji}) = \sum \mathbf{F}_i^{ext}$. Consequences: a system at rest with no external resultant force has a fixed COM forever; a moving system's COM continues on a straight line (source E2:

cards.title: M a_cm = F_ext: the only equation of motion for a system (cont.)
items: the COM of an exploding shell follows the original parabola - gravity never noticed the explosion).

Explosions and recoil (source E2, Q2): a shell of mass $M$ bursts into fragments; the COM continues along the pre-burst trajectory. If a 4 kg mass moving east at 6 m/s explodes into 2 kg moving west at 3 m/s, momentum gives $24 = 2(-3) + 2v \Rightarrow v = 15$ m/s east for the other 2 kg piece.
the 2 kg piece moves at 6 m/s west and the COM keeps going - the exact numbers per the source's configuration; the ledger is always $\sum m_i \mathbf{v}_i = M\mathbf{v}_{cm}$ = conserved.

cards.title: M a_cm = F_ext: the only equation of motion for a system (cont.)
items: Statics via COM: if the COM hangs directly below the suspension point, the net torque about the suspension is zero and the body is in equilibrium. Tension/string problems: the string's line passes through the COM of the hanging system (source Q25-family statics).

the internal forces cancel PAIRWISE - no cancellation is ever lost no matter how violent the explosion or how complicated the contact. This is why the COM path is the invariant of every collision and explosion problem.

E2 audit: projectile motion of the COM continues unaffected; if your fragment trajectories give a COM that leaves the parabola, momentum was mis-accounted. Q2 numbers: total p before $= 24$ kg m/s east; after $= 2(-3) + 2(15) = 24$ ok.

cards.title: Conservation of momentum: the conditions
items: $\sum \mathbf{p}_{before} = \sum \mathbf{p}_{after}$ holds when the net external IMPULSE over the interaction vanishes: (1) no external forces at all, or (2) external forces cancel, or (3) the collision is so brief that $\int \mathbf{F}_{ext} dt \approx 0$ over the contact (the standard exam licence). Momentum is a VECTOR: conserve component by component;
a wall's normal force can kill the perpendicular component while the parallel component survives (CM-21).

title: M a_cm = F_ext: the only equation of motion for a system
subtitle: System form of Newton 2; conservation conditions; explosion/recoil; traps.
takeaway: M a_cm = F_ext: internal forces cancel in pairs; an explosion scatters fragments around an unperturbed COM path.

cards.title: Conservation of momentum: the conditions (cont.)
items: System choice matters: pick the system so that the interesting forces are internal. Bullet + block: momentum conserved (gravity/normal cancel over the brief contact). Block + Earth (pendulum swing): momentum NOT conserved (the pivot pulls), but energy is. State the system before writing the equation - examiners award the statement.

The COM fixed-point theorem: if total momentum is zero (initially at rest), the COM stays put no matter the internal rearrangement - man on boat (CM-19), explosion at rest (CM-05), spring release (CM-14).

cards.title: Conservation of momentum: the conditions (cont.)
items: each conservation claim must name its axis: 'horizontal momentum conserved' because the floor's normal and gravity are vertical. Silent assumptions lose marks.

(a) 3 kg and 5 kg connected by a compressed spring on a smooth floor, released: $3v_1 + 5v_2 = 0$: velocities are in the ratio $5:3$ opposite. (b) A man at one end of a 4 kg boat walks to the other end: the COM of man\boat stays fixed horizontally (CM-19). (c) A ball falls and bounces elastically off the floor:

cards.title: COM motion drills (cont.)
items: during the bounce the floor's external impulse changes the SYSTEM momentum (Earth + ball conserves it); the ball alone does not.

(d) Rocket in free space: no external force, so $v_{cm}$ of rocket\exhaust is constant; the exhaust's momentum balances the rocket's gain (CM-17). (e) Explosion of a 6 kg projectile at the top of its flight into 2 kg and 4 kg: both pieces fall with $g$; the COM stays on the original parabola (source E2).

cards.title: COM motion drills (cont.)
items: drill (a): $v_1 = -5v_2/3$ - the light piece moves faster in the inverse ratio ok; total p zero before and after ok.

Trap: $M a_{cm} = F_{ext}$ does NOT say each piece follows $F_{ext}$; it says the average does. Trap: 'internal forces are always small' - no, they can be huge; they simply cancel. Trap: using the law across a time when an external impulse acts (the pendulum pivot, the wall, friction): the COM accelerates then and momentum is not conserved.

title: M a_cm = F_ext: the only equation of motion for a system (cont.)
subtitle: System form of Newton 2; conservation conditions; explosion/recoil; traps.
takeaway: M a_cm = F_ext: internal forces cancel in pairs; an explosion scatters fragments around an unperturbed COM path.

cards.title: Traps specific to the system law (cont.)
items: Trap: forgetting a mass in $M$ (the classic half-included hanging chain - count only the moving subsystem; for variable-mass chains use the flux ledger (CM-18)). Trap: treating $v_{cm}$ as the velocity of every part after an explosion - only the MEAN is that.
the 30-second audit for any problem: what is the system? what external forces act? does their impulse matter on this time scale? then choose conservation or not.

Scenario 1 - explosion/recoil at rest: total p = 0 stays 0; fragment momenta are equal and opposite. 4 kg at rest explodes into 2.5 kg and 1.5 kg: $2.5v_1 = -1.5v_2$: speeds in the ratio $1.5 : 2.5 = 3 : 5$. Scenario 2 - projectile explosion at the top (source E2): horizontal momentum conserved through the burst; gravity sets the COM parabola.

cards.title: Standard conservation scenarios (Q2, Q17, Q22, P22)
items: Scenario 3 - two skaters push apart (source Q17-family): $m_1v_1 = -m_2v_2$ in the COM sense; speeds inverse to masses.

Scenario 4 - bullet into block (P22): $m v_0 = (m + M)V$; the pair then swings (CM-13). Scenario 5 - ball off a wedge on a smooth floor: horizontal momentum conserved; the wedge recoils so that $m v_x + M V = $ const; the COM stays fixed horizontally (CM-19). Scenario 6 - collision on a smooth surface with frictionless supports (P26): conserve the free component; name the constrained one.

cards.title: Standard conservation scenarios (Q2, Q17, Q22, P22)
items: Scenario 7 - man on boat (Q10, E8): fixed COM displacements. Scenario 8 - spring released between blocks (Q18, corrected): zero total momentum + spring energy = shared KE (CM-14). Every one of these is 'choose the system, kill the internal forces, project on the free axis'.

conservation is not a formula but a BOOKKEEPING CHOICE: system, axis, time window. Made correctly, the rest is arithmetic; made silently, the classic errors (energy across collisions, momentum across swings) appear.

Q2 audit: before $= 24$ kg m/s; after: piece 1 west at 3 m/s carries $-6$; the 2 kg piece must carry $+30$: $v = 15$ m/s east; COM speed before and after is the same $24/4 = 6$ m/s for the 4 kg system.

cards.title: Momentum with external forces present: the impulse window
items: When external forces act, momentum conservation still applies if the external IMPULSE over the window is negligible: collision contact times (ms) make gravity's $mg\Delta t$ tiny - the exam licence. When the window is long (swing, slide), momentum is NOT conserved but energy may be. The two-stage protocol (CM-13) is this dichotomy in action.

Friction window: a block sliding on a rough floor has momentum destroyed by $\mu mg t$; if the problem asks for speeds after a slide, use work-energy instead. Explosion on a rough surface: conserve momentum THROUGH the explosion (brief), then let friction work on each piece separately.

title: The standard conservation scenarios (source Q2, Q17, Q22, P22, P26)
subtitle: Eight standard scenarios; impulse windows; system choice; drills.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. 3.5 / Q2 Q17; independently checked
takeaway: Total momentum is conserved when the net external impulse vanishes, component by component.

cards.title: Momentum with external forces present: the impulse window (cont.)
items: Water/rocket windows: variable-mass problems use the $dt$ ledger (CM-16/17) - momentum of the chosen system plus flux terms; never mix the flux ledger with the closed-system shortcut silently.
window audit: state 'contact time is short so external impulse is negligible' before using conservation - that sentence is the licence.

(a) Ball bounces off the floor: system = ball alone: floor impulse external, momentum not conserved. System = ball + Earth: conserved (and huge mass makes the recoil unmeasurable). (b) Bullet through block (Q19): system = bullet + block: horizontal p conserved through the passage ok; energy is not (1045 J to heat).

cards.title: Choosing the system: worked contrasts (cont.)
items: (c) Two blocks and a spring on ice: system = both + spring: p conserved, and mechanical energy conserved (smooth spring) - the rare case where BOTH hold. (d) Cart under a hopper (OLY-10): system = cart + dropped sand column: horizontal p conserved; the loading force $\dot m v$ is internal to the widened system.
one-liner test: 'could an external force deliver a noticeable impulse during the event?' If yes and you used conservation, the answer is wrong.

cards.title: Conservation drills
items: (a) 5 kg cart at 4 m/s picks up 5 kg dropped from rest: $v = 20/10 = 2$ m/s. (b) 3 kg at 6 east collides and sticks to 2 kg at 4 west: $18 - 8 = 10 = 5v$: $v = 2$ m/s east. (c) 0.5 kg ball at 10 hits 1.5 kg at rest, $e = 0.5$: $v_2 = (1+e)m_1u_1/(m_1+m_2) = 1.5(0.5)(10)/2 = 3.75$ m/s; $v_1 = (0.5-0.75)10/2 = -1.25$ m/s (rebounds).
(d) Two ice skaters 60 and 90 kg push to relative 3 m/s: $60v_1 = 90v_2$, $v_1 + v_2 = 3$: $v_2 = 1.2$, $v_1 = 1.8$ m/s.

cards.title: Conservation drills (cont.)
items: Definitions: ELASTIC = kinetic energy conserved, $e = 1$. PERFECTLY INELASTIC = the bodies stick (maximum KE loss consistent with momentum), $e = 0$. INELASTIC = anything between, $0 < e < 1$. SUPERELASTIC = $e > 1$ with a released spring/explosive - possible, and energy GAINS. The coefficient of RESTITUTION measures speeds along the line of impact:

title: Elastic, inelastic, sticking: one number e prices every collision
subtitle: Restitution definition and scope; line of impact; deformation/reformation impulses; drills.
takeaway: Elastic means e = 1; sticking means e = 0; e measures separation speed over approach speed along the line of impact.

cards.title: Elastic, inelastic, sticking: restitution e (cont.)
items: $e = \dfrac{v_{sep}}{v_{app}} = \dfrac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}$ (1-D; see CM-11 for the 2-D projection).

Why $e$ is about speeds not velocities: it is defined on the components along the common normal at contact. For smooth bodies the tangential components are untouched; friction is the only channel across (source trap). Material dependence: $e$ varies with speed and temperature; the exam treats it as a given constant per problem. Energy is a derived quantity here: $e$ and momentum decide the outcome; energy then reports the bill (CM-09).

cards.title: Elastic, inelastic, sticking: restitution e (cont.)
items: Sticking = the INELASTIC limit: after contact the bodies share $v_{cm}$ - the only outcome consistent with zero separation speed and momentum conservation. Perfectly inelastic is NOT 'maximum energy destroyed' in one number - it is 'minimum final KE' subject to the momentum ledger; the lost amount is exactly $K_{rel}$ (CM-09).

the separation/definition choice makes the whole classification one dimensionless number; every exam question about 'what kind of collision' reduces to (i) what is $e$ and (ii) where is the line of impact.

limits: $e = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 = v_1 = v_{cm}$ ok; $e = 1 \Rightarrow$ energy conserved ok (verify with the master formulas of CM-07); $e > 1 \Rightarrow$ post-collision KE exceeds pre - flag it as superelastic rather than erroring.

cards.title: The line of impact (source C1-C2 family)
items: For SPHERES the line of impact is the line joining centres at the moment of contact. The plane of contact is perpendicular to it. $e$ applies along the line of impact ONLY. For a smooth wall the line of impact is the wall normal. For rough bodies or spinning balls, tangential impulses exist and $e$ no longer closes the system alone - the problem needs friction data.

Angle traps (source C9, corrected): a ball bouncing off a smooth wall leaves at angle $\theta_r$ with $\tan\theta_r = \tan\theta_i / e$ from the normal - MORE grazing for $e < 1$; equal angles iff $e = 1$. The mirrored-bounce picture is the elastic-only special case (full correction in CM-22).

cards.title: The line of impact (source C1-C2 family) (cont.)
items: 2-D bookkeeping (CM-11): project velocities onto the line of impact, apply momentum + $e$ there, leave tangential components unchanged, recompose. The whole of oblique-collision theory is this three-step recipe.
draw the contact configuration FIRST: the line of impact is geometry, not choice. A wrong line poisons every later equation.

Every direct impact has two phases. DEFORMATION: the bodies squish to a common velocity $v_{cm}$; the impulse so far is $J_d = \mu u_{rel}$ (exactly what kills the relative velocity). REFORMATION: elastic recovery pushes them apart with impulse $J_r = e\,\mu u_{rel}$. Total contact impulse on each body along the line: $J = (1+e)\mu u_{rel}$.

title: Elastic, inelastic, sticking: one number e prices every collision (cont.)
subtitle: Restitution definition and scope; line of impact; deformation/reformation impulses; drills.
takeaway: Elastic means e = 1; sticking means e = 0; e measures separation speed over approach speed along the line of impact.

cards.title: Impulse of deformation & reformation (Cengage 1.22)
items: Energy reading: at maximum deformation ALL the relative KE $\frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2$ is stored; recovery returns the fraction $e^2$; what never returns is $\frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2(1-e^2)$. Sticking ($e = 0$) has no reformation phase at all; elastic ($e = 1$) has $J_r = J_d$ and returns everything.

cards.title: Impulse of deformation & reformation (Cengage 1.22)
items: Why $J_d = \mu u_{rel}$ is pure mechanics: at max deformation both bodies share $v_{cm}$ (momentum fixes it whatever the contact law); the impulse that took $(u_1, u_2) \to (v_{cm}, v_{cm})$ is $m_1(v_{cm} - u_1) = -\mu u_{rel}$. Only $J_r = e J_d$ is the material's business.
2 kg at 5 into 3 kg rest, $e = 0.6$: $J_d = 6$, $J_r = 3.6$, $J = 9.6$ N s; velocities $v_1 = 0.2$, $v_2 = 3.2$; impulse on 3 kg $= 9.6$ ok matches $J$.

cards.title: Classification drills and traps
items: (a) 1 kg at 8 sticks to 3 kg at rest: $v_{cm} = 2$; lost $= K_{rel} = \frac{1}{2}(0.75)(64) = 24$ J; $K_i = 32$, $K_f = 8$: loss 24 ok ($e = 0$). (b) Same masses elastic: $v_1 = -4$, $v_2 = 4$; energy conserved ok. (c) $e = 0.7$ version: $v_1 = (1-2.1)8/4 = -2.2$; $v_2 = 1.7(1)(8)/4 = 3.4$; $e$-check $(3.4+2.2)/8 = 0.7$ ok.

Trap: 'inelastic means the bodies stick' - only PERFECTLY inelastic does. Trap: using $e$ for energy directly - $e$ is a speed ratio; energy scales as $e^2$. Trap: applying $e$ to the full speed in 2-D instead of the normal component.

cards.title: Classification drills and traps (cont.)
items: drill (a) fraction: equal masses lose exactly HALF the KE when sticking ($K_{cm} = K_{rel}$ split) ok - a favourite true/false.

Momentum: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = m_1v_1 + m_2v_2$. Restitution: $v_2 - v_1 = e(u_1 - u_2)$. Solve the pair for the master formulas: $v_1 = \dfrac{(m_1 - e m_2)u_1 + (1+e)m_2 u_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ and $v_2 = \dfrac{(1+e)m_1 u_1 + (m_2 - e m_1)u_2}{m_1 + m_2}$.
Valid in 1-D (or along the line of impact in 2-D) for fixed masses; $e$ given; no external impulse.

title: The pair that prices every 1-D collision
subtitle: Master formulas 3.7a/b; three-invariant audit; P32 worked; drills.
takeaway: One pair of equations prices every 1-D collision: momentum conservation plus v2 - v1 = -e (u1 - u2).

cards.title: The pair that prices every 1-D collision (cont.)
items: Memory anchors: the shooter's own mass enters its numerator with MINUS $e$ times the target's; the target's velocity is dragged in with $+(1+e)$; the denominator is always the total mass. Limits: $e = 0$ gives both velocities $= v_{cm}$ ok; $e = 1$, $m_1 = m_2$ gives $v_1 = u_2$, $v_2 = u_1$ (the exchange) ok; $m_2 \gg m_1$ gives $v_1 \approx -u_1 + 2u_2$ (the wall) ok.

Relative-velocity form: $v_{rel} = -e\,u_{rel}$ with $u_{rel} = u_1 - u_2$ - one line, sign-sensitive. Combined with $v_{cm}$ fixed by momentum, this reconstructs both velocities faster than the formulas when $u_2 = 0$ or masses are equal. The CM frame (CM-15) is the same pair in geometric dress.

cards.title: The pair that prices every 1-D collision (cont.)
items: the pair is complete: two equations, two unknowns. $e$ is the only place material physics enters; everything else is conservation. Any collision answer that violates either equation is simply wrong.

three-invariant audit for every computed answer: (1) signed momentum, (2) $e = (v_2-v_1)/(u_1-u_2)$, (3) energy ledger (CM-09). The trio catches sign slips, mis-multiplied factors, and wrong-mass errors.

cards.title: Worked with the invariants: the P32 set (source) (cont.)
items: Arithmetic discipline: the factor $(1+e)$ multiplies the WHOLE $m_2u_2$ term ($1.5 \times 3 \times (-2) = -9$, not $-15$); one dropped factor here produced the source's Q18 slip family. Write the numerator terms with their factors before multiplying.
if any of the three invariants fails, recompute - do not adjust the answer to fit. The three together pin the solution uniquely.

cards.title: Drill set (each: compute, then audit)
Drill set (each: compute, then audit) (cont.)
Drill set (each: compute, then audit) (cont.)
items: Two contacts at once (a wedge between two balls): solve the constraints together or sequentially with clear stages. Variable mass: use the flux ledger (CM-16). Extended bodies with spin: angular impulse needed (rigid-body chapter). Explosions: $e$ is meaningless (no contact) - use momentum + energy release. 2-D: project first (CM-11).

The formulas also fail if $e$ is velocity-dependent (real materials at high speed): then the problem must give $e$ at the relevant speed or an energy loss directly. State the constant-$e$ assumption when using them.

cards.title: When the master formulas are the wrong tool (cont.)
items: tool-selection audit: does the problem have ONE contact, two fixed masses, and a stated $e$? If yes use the masters; if not, fall back to first principles.

CASE 1 - equal masses, elastic ($e = 1$): VELOCITIES EXCHANGE: $v_1 = u_2$, $v_2 = u_1$ (source E3). One stops if the other was at rest - in 1-D only; in 2-D the equal-mass elastic result is the 90-degree separation (CM-12). CASE 2 - equal masses, any $e$: $v_1 = \frac{(1-e)}{2}u_1 + \frac{(1+e)}{2}u_2$ and vice versa - the symmetric split.

cards.title: Special cases worth recognising on sight (cont.)
items: CASE 3 - heavy target ($m_2 \gg m_1$): $v_1 \approx (1-e)u_2 - e u_1 + $ corrections; for a wall at rest: $v_1 \approx -e u_1$ (rebounds scaled), $v_2 \approx 0$ (wall barely moves). CASE 4 - light target ($m_1 \gg m_2$): $v_1 \approx u_1$ (plows on), $v_2 \approx (1+e)u_1 - e u_2 \approx 2u_1$ for resting light target and $e = 1$ - the light flies at nearly TWICE the heavy's speed. Q21-set (source):
heavy into light elastic: the light piece's speed is nearly $2u$ and the heavy barely slows (source prints $-2$ / $1$ for its configuration).

cards.title: Special cases worth recognising on sight (cont.)
items: CASE 5 - sticking: $v = v_{cm}$ for both. CASE 6 - projectile vs equal target at rest with $e$: $v_1 = \frac{(1-e)}{2}u$, $v_2 = \frac{(1+e)}{2}u$ - memorise this pair; many drills specialise it. CASE 7 - target moving toward shooter: use the full formulas; the relative-velocity form $v_{rel} = -e u_{rel}$ plus $v_{cm}$ is fastest.

the cases are the master formulas seen in their natural limits; recognising them converts a 3-minute derive into a 20-second quote - with the derivation still available if the numbers don't match a case.

cards.title: Q11 worked (the detective problem, source)
items: Ball A of mass $m$ at speed $u$ strikes ball B (mass $m$) at rest; after, A moves at $u/3$ at angle $\theta_1$ (Q11): use the master formulas + the 90-degree theorem (CM-12) to pin the outcome: for equal masses elastic 2-D, $\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90$ and $v_1 = u\cos\theta_1$, $v_2 = u\sin\theta_1$; given one post speed or angle, the rest follows from the momentum triangle.

Method (any Q11-type): (1) check the 90-degree conditions; (2) draw the momentum triangle ($\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2$); (3) quote the two speeds as components of $u$; (4) audit KE. If the masses differ or $e < 1$, drop the theorem and run the CM-frame machinery (OLY-02).

title: Special cases worth recognising on sight
subtitle: Equal-mass exchange, heavy/light limits, sticking; Q11 method; contrast drills.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. 3.7 / E3 Q3 Q11; independently checked
takeaway: Equal masses exchange velocities only in 1-D elastic; heavy barely slows; light bounces at nearly 2u1 - u2.

cards.title: Q11 worked (the detective problem, source) (cont.)
items: sanity: for any angle the two speeds satisfy $v_1^2 + v_2^2 = u^2$ (elastic equal-mass) - the circle of possible outcomes has radius $u$.
1 kg at 8 into 3 kg at rest, $e = 1$: $v_1 = (1-3)8/4 = -4$ (rebounds); $v_2 = 2(1)(8)/4 = 4$; loss 0 ok. Same with $e = 0$: both at 2 m/s; loss $= 24 = \frac{1}{2}(0.75)(64)$ ok.

cards.title: Contrast drills: same masses, different e (cont.)
items: the trend table: as $e$ falls from 1 to 0, the shooter's rebound fades into forward drift at $v_{cm}$ and the energy loss rises from 0 to $K_{rel}$ monotonically ok.

(a) equal masses, elastic, one at rest: exchange. (b) heavy hits light elastic at rest: light flies at $\approx 2u$. (c) light hits heavy at rest, $e = 1$: light rebounds at $\approx u$. (d) perfectly inelastic any masses: common $v_{cm}$. (e) equal masses elastic 2-D: 90 degrees.
Warning: case 1 is 1-D ONLY (source P5's ambiguity; corrected reading in CM-22); case 3's $2u$ needs $e = 1$; case 5's energy loss is $K_{rel}$, not 'all the energy'.

cards.title: Recognition drills (60 seconds each) (cont.)
items: self-test: state each case's hypotheses before its conclusion - the hypotheses ARE the exam points.

Decompose the KE: $K = \frac{1}{2}Mv_{cm}^2 + \frac{1}{2}\mu v_{rel}^2$ with $\mu = \dfrac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ (CM-15). Momentum conservation freezes $v_{cm}$; restitution sets $v_{rel}^{after} = -e\,v_{rel}^{before}$. The collision can only spend the relative part:
$K_{loss} = \frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2(1 - e^2)$ with $u_{rel} = u_1 - u_2$ (source 3.8, P32).

cards.title: K_loss = 1/2 mu (u1-u2)^2 (1-e^2): the complete energy bill (cont.
items: Reading the formula: the STAKE is $K_{rel} = \frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2$ (the reduced mass and the approach speed); the FRACTION spent is $1 - e^2$ (not $1 - e$). $e = 1$: nothing lost; $e = 0$: the whole $K_{rel}$ gone; superelastic $e > 1$: negative loss = energy released (a spring). The $K_{cm}$ term is untouchable - sticking still leaves $\frac{1}{2}Mv_{cm}^2$ moving.

Worked (P32 numbers): $\mu = 1.2$, $u_{rel} = 7$, $e = 0.5$: $K_{loss} = \frac{1}{2}(1.2)(49)(0.75) = 22.05$ J ok equals $K_i - K_f = 31 - 8.95$ from the master formulas (CM-07). Equal masses sticking: $\mu = m/2$, $u_{rel} = u$: loss $= \frac{1}{4}mu^2 = \frac{1}{2}K_i$ - HALF the energy, the classic true/false (source trap).

title: K_loss = 1/2 mu (u1-u2)^2 (1-e^2): the complete energy bill
subtitle: K_loss formula and derivation; two-stage ledgers; reduced mass; drills.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. 3.7-3.8 / E4 P32; independently checked
takeaway: K_loss = 1/2 mu (u1 - u2)^2 (1 - e^2): the reduced mass and approach speed set the stake; e sets the loss.

cards.title: K_loss = 1/2 mu (u1-u2)^2 (1-e^2): the complete energy bill (cont.
items: the decomposition is exact for two bodies (parallel-axis theorem for KE): $\sum \frac{1}{2}m_i v_i^2 = \frac{1}{2}Mv_{cm}^2 + \frac{1}{2}\mu v_{rel}^2$; the cross terms vanish because $\sum m_i \mathbf{v}'_i = 0$. So the collision's budget is literally $K_{rel}$.

E4 (source): 4 kg at 6 into a wall... the perfectly inelastic pair loses $K_{rel}$: 4 kg at 6 sticks to 1 kg: $\mu = 0.8$, $u_{rel} = 6$: loss $= \frac{1}{2}(0.8)(36) = 14.4$ J; $K_i = 72$, $v = 4.8$, $K_f = 57.6$; loss 14.4 ok. Source E4 prints 183.8 J for its own configuration - same formula.

cards.title: Energy ledgers in two-stage problems
items: Ballistic pendulum (CM-13): stage-1 loss $= K_{rel}$ with $\mu \approx m_{bullet}$; the surviving fraction $m/(m+M)$ of the bullet KE then converts to $mgh$ (E5: 800 J in, 3.98 J swing, 796 J heat = 99.5%). Bullet through block (Q19): $K_i = 1250$, $K_f = 204.5$: 1045.5 J heat. Spring problems (CM-14): the collision's loss and the spring's share must be booked separately.

Superelastic bookkeeping: if $e > 1$ or a spring releases during contact, $K_{loss} < 0$; write $K_{gain} = \frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2(e^2-1)$ and state the source of the energy. Explosions: $\Delta K = +$ chemical/spring release (source E2): no restitution involved.

cards.title: Energy ledgers in two-stage problems (cont.)
items: double-entry: compute the loss both from $K_i - K_f$ (master formulas) and from $\frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2(1-e^2)$; they must agree to rounding (P32: 22.05 both ways).

$\mu = m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$: smaller than either mass; for equal masses $m$: $\mu = m/2$; for $m_2 \gg m_1$: $\mu \approx m_1$ (the light one sets the scale); symmetric in the two bodies. $M = m_1 + m_2$ for the COM term.

The pair $(M, \mu)$ is the natural coordinates of two-body motion - the same $\mu$ appears in the relative-coordinate equation $\mu a_{rel} = F_{internal}$ and in spring oscillations of two-body systems.

cards.title: The reduced mass itself (cont.)
items: Limits: $\mu \to 0$ when one mass vanishes (no collision stake); $\mu \to m/2$ for equal; $1/\mu = 1/m_1 + 1/m_2$ (the harmonic flavour). Drill: 3 kg and 6 kg: $\mu = 2$ kg; 1 kg and 1 kg: 0.5; 1 kg and 1000 kg: 0.999.
dimension: $\mu$ is a mass; $\frac{1}{2}\mu v^2$ an energy ok; the loss formula is never negative for $|e| \leqslant 1$ ok.

title: K_loss = 1/2 mu (u1-u2)^2 (1-e^2): the complete energy bill (cont.)
subtitle: K_loss formula and derivation; two-stage ledgers; reduced mass; drills.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. 3.7-3.8 / E4 P32; independently checked
takeaway: K_loss = 1/2 mu (u1 - u2)^2 (1 - e^2): the reduced mass and approach speed set the stake; e sets the loss.

cards.title: Loss-formula drills (cont.)
items: Trap: using $1 - e$ instead of $1 - e^2$; using $m_1 + m_2$ instead of $\mu$; forgetting $u_{rel}$ is SIGNED before squaring (sign dies in the square - but keep it for the $e$-check).
cross-audit every drill against the master-formula difference; the two routes agreeing is the exam's strongest check.

A direct impact has two phases. Phase 1 DEFORMATION: the bodies approach at $u_{rel} = u_1 - u_2$, squish, and reach a common velocity $v_{cm}$ at the instant of maximum deformation. The impulse delivered by contact so far is $J_d = \mu u_{rel}$ (exactly what is needed to kill the relative velocity: after it, both bodies move at $v_{cm}$). Phase 2 REFORMATION: elastic recovery pushes them apart;

cards.title: Deformation and reformation impulses (cont.)
items: the reformation impulse is $J_r = e\,\mu u_{rel}$. Total contact impulse on each body: $J = J_d + J_r = (1+e)\mu u_{rel}$, directed along the line of impact.

Why $J_d = \mu u_{rel}$: at maximum deformation both bodies share one velocity $v$; momentum conservation fixes $v = v_{cm}$ regardless of the contact law. The impulse that took the pair from $(u_1, u_2)$ to $(v_{cm}, v_{cm})$ is $m_1(v_{cm} - u_1) = -\mu u_{rel}$ on body 1 (and opposite on body 2) - pure algebra from momentum, no material assumption.

cards.title: Deformation and reformation impulses (cont.)
items: Then the reformation is the material-dependent part: the contact force history after the peak, with impulse scaled by $e$.

Energy story (this is where the $1-e^2$ comes from): at maximum deformation the ENTIRE relative KE $\frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2$ has been extracted (stored as deformation energy in the contact). Recovery returns a fraction $e^2$ of it ($\frac{1}{2}\mu(e u_{rel})^2$ of relative KE after separation). What never comes back: $\frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2(1-e^2)$ = the permanent loss.
For sticking ($e = 0$) there is no phase 2 at all; for elastic ($e = 1$) phase 2 returns everything and $J_r = J_d$.

cards.title: Deformation and reformation impulses (cont.)
items: the decomposition isolates the material law in ONE number ($e$) while phase 1 is universal mechanics. It also answers 'maximum compression of the spring between the carts' questions: at max deformation the spring holds ALL of the former relative KE; equate $\frac{1}{2}k x_{max}^2 = \frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2$ (CM-14).

impulse route reproduces the master formulas: $v_1 = u_1 - J/m_1$, $v_2 = u_2 + J/m_2$ with $J = (1+e)\mu u_{rel}$ gives (3.7a-b) term by term. Elastic equal masses: $J = 2\mu u = mu$; shooter: $u - mu/m = 0$ stops; target: $0 + mu/m = u$ takes the speed.

title: Two impulses inside every collision: deformation and reformation
subtitle: Deformation and reformation impulses J_d = mu u_rel, J_r = e J_d; energy return e^2; peak compression.
takeaway: Deformation impulse mu u_app stores the relative KE; a fraction e^2 springs back; (1 + e) mu u_app is the total jolt.

cards.title: Numbers: J_d, J_r and the peak-force language
items: 2 kg at 5 m/s hits 3 kg at rest with $e = 0.6$: $u_{rel} = 5$, $\mu = 1.2$. $J_d = 1.2\times5 = 6$ N s; $J_r = 0.6\times6 = 3.6$ N s; $J = 9.6$ N s. Check via velocities: $v_1 = (2-1.8)5/5 = 0.2$ m/s; $v_2 = 1.6\times2\times5/5 = 3.2$ m/s. Impulse on 2 kg: $2(0.2-5) = -9.6$ N s equals $-J$; on 3 kg: $3(3.2) = 9.6$.

cards.title: Numbers: J_d, J_r and the peak-force language (cont.)
items: Peak contact force: at the deformation instant the relative speed is zero and the spring-like contact is maximally compressed - that is where the largest force acts. If a problem quotes an average force over contact time $\Delta t$: $\bar F = J/\Delta t$; if it quotes a spring constant for the contact: $\frac{1}{2}kx_{max}^2 = \frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2$ and $x_{max}$ occurs at $v_{cm}$ (same instant).
The deformation instant is the answer to 'when is the spring fully compressed' questions.

cards.title: Numbers: J_d, J_r and the peak-force language (cont.)
items: deformation-phase energy audit on the numbers above: $K_i = 25$ J; at $v_{cm} = 2$ m/s: $K = \frac{1}{2}(5)(4) = 10$ J; extracted $= 15$ J $= \frac{1}{2}(1.2)(25) = 15$ J $= K_{rel}$. After reformation: $K_f = \frac{1}{2}2(0.04) + \frac{1}{2}3(10.24) = 15.4$ J; returned $= 5.4$ J $= e^2 K_{rel} = 0.36\times15$. Lost $= 9.6$ J $= 15(1-0.36)$.

the Cengage floor names these the impulse of deformation ($J_d$) and impulse of reformation ($J_r$) in section 1.22; the source chapter does not treat them explicitly - added here as core JEE mechanics.

cards.title: Where the phase picture is used
items: (1) Spring between carts: max compression at the deformation instant when both move at $v_{cm}$; energy $= K_{rel}$ stored; then release. If the contact is perfectly elastic, the spring returns all of it and the carts separate with $e = 1$ formulas. (2) Squeezing force questions: 'what is the maximum force during contact' - use the contact spring law at $x_{max}$. (3) Two-stage contact:
two carts with a bumper of $e$ then a stop - apply the impulse ledger stage by stage.

(4) Sticking clay: $J = J_d$ only; the whole $K_{rel}$ becomes heat. (5) Real materials: $e < 1$ because the contact hysteresis loop is smaller than the loading loop - $J_r < J_d$; the ratio $J_r/J_d = e$ IS the restitution coefficient in impulse language.

title: Two impulses inside every collision: deformation and reformation (cont.)
subtitle: Deformation and reformation impulses J_d = mu u_rel, J_r = e J_d; energy return e^2; peak compression.
takeaway: Deformation impulse mu u_app stores the relative KE; a fraction e^2 springs back; (1 + e) mu u_app is the total jolt.

cards.title: Where the phase picture is used (cont.)
items: the phase picture survives even when the contact is not a linear spring: $J_d = \mu u_{rel}$ is pure momentum; only $J_r = e J_d$ is empirical. That is why the same formulas describe clay, steel and rubber.
extremes: $e = 0$: $J = \mu u_{rel}$, no return; $e = 1$: $J = 2\mu u_{rel}$, full return. The total impulse is always linear in $(1+e)$ - a useful graph: $J$ vs $e$ is a straight line.

cards.title: Micro-set: impulse-decomposition drills (cont.)
items: (b) Sticking pair 2 kg at 6 into 2 kg at rest: $\mu = 1$, $J = J_d = 6$ N s; common speed 3 m/s. (c) Elastic equal-mass exchange: $J = 2\mu u = mu$; the deformation and reformation impulses are equal halves of the contact jolt.

cards.title: Oblique collisions: decompose on the line of impact
items: For smooth spheres the collision force is purely normal (no friction), so the recipe is fixed: (1) draw the line of impact (the line joining centres at contact) and the plane of contact (perpendicular to it); (2) project both velocities onto the line of impact - these 1-D components obey momentum + $e$ EXACTLY as in CM-07; (3) the components perpendicular to the line of impact (tangential) are UNCHANGED for each body;
(4) recompose. Momentum is conserved in both directions, but restitution speaks only along the normal.

cards.title: Oblique collisions: decompose on the line of impact (cont.)
items: Bookkeeping form: label the line of impact as $n$ and the tangent as $t$. Then $v_{1n} = \frac{(m_1 - e m_2)u_{1n} + (1+e)m_2 u_{2n}}{m_1+m_2}$, $v_{2n} = \frac{(1+e)m_1 u_{1n} + (m_2 - e m_1)u_{2n}}{m_1+m_2}$, while $v_{1t} = u_{1t}$, $v_{2t} = u_{2t}$. Four scalars in, four out. If the target is at rest, $u_{2n} = u_{2t} = 0$ and the formulas simplify to the zero-target pair of CM-07 along $n$.

The geometry trap: the line of impact is NOT horizontal unless the geometry says so. For a sphere hitting a fixed inclined plane, the line of impact is the plane normal; for two spheres, it is the line of centres - which depends on the impact parameter (how grazing the hit is). Draw the contact configuration first; every later equation hangs off that line.

title: Oblique collisions: decompose on the line of impact
subtitle: Line of impact decomposition; tangential invariance; wall and incline cases; drills.
takeaway: Resolve along the line of impact (momentum + e) and perpendicular to it (unchanged for smooth spheres).

cards.title: Oblique collisions: decompose on the line of impact (cont.)
items: Angles in the final answer are measured from whatever axis the problem states - recompose then project.

tangential velocities survive because the third-law pair of contact forces acts along the common normal - friction is the only channel into $t$, and smoothness closes it. This independence is what makes 2-D decomposable into a 1-D problem plus free streaming.

recompose-energy sanity for elastic smooth collisions: KE is conserved iff the normal parts conserve it (they do by $e = 1$) and the tangentials are unchanged (they are). If your 2-D elastic answer fails a KE check, the projection angle is wrong.

cards.title: Worked template: at-rest target, impact parameter set by geomet.
items: A sphere $m_1$ moving horizontally at $u$ strikes an identical sphere $m_2$ at rest; the line of centres at contact makes angle $\phi$ with the original direction (impact parameter $b = (R_1+R_2)\sin\phi$ for centre separation $R_1+R_2$). Decompose: $u_{1n} = u\cos\phi$, $u_{1t} = u\sin\phi$, target zero. Elastic equal masses along $n$: exchange the normal components: $v_{1n} = 0$, $v_{2n} = u\cos\phi$;

cards.title: Worked template: at-rest target, impact parameter set by geometr.
items: Recompose: shooter leaves with speed $u\sin\phi$ perpendicular to the line of centres; target with $u\cos\phi$ along the line of centres. The two are PERPENDICULAR - this is the 90-degree theorem of CM-12 in general clothing. For $\phi \to 0$ (head-on) the shooter stops; for $\phi \to 90$ degrees (grazing) nothing happens;
the scattering angle of the shooter is $90 - \phi$ from its original line.

cards.title: Worked template: at-rest target, impact parameter set by geometr.
items: With restitution $e$ and equal masses: $v_{1n} = \frac{(1-e)}{2}u\cos\phi$ from the master: $v_{1n} = \frac{(m-em)u\cos\phi}{2m} = \frac{(1-e)}{2}u\cos\phi$; $v_{2n} = \frac{(1+e)}{2}u\cos\phi$. Then $v_{1t} = u\sin\phi$ untouched. The shooter's speed after:
$\sqrt{u^2\sin^2\phi + \frac{(1-e)^2}{4}u^2\cos^2\phi}$ - note only the normal part is taxed by $e$.

title: Oblique collisions: decompose on the line of impact (cont.)
subtitle: Line of impact decomposition; tangential invariance; wall and incline cases; drills.
takeaway: Resolve along the line of impact (momentum + e) and perpendicular to it (unchanged for smooth spheres).

cards.title: Worked template: at-rest target, impact parameter set by geometr.
items: the $e = 1$, $\phi = 0$ limit gives $v_1 = 0$, $v_2 = u$ (head-on exchange). The $\phi = 90$ degrees limit gives $v_1 = u$, $v_2 = 0$ (no collision). Both limits of the general formula are physically obvious - a good memorisation anchor.

Ball hits a fixed smooth wall at angle $\theta$ from the normal with speed $v$: tangential $= v\sin\theta$ unchanged; normal $= v\cos\theta$ becomes $-e v\cos\theta$ (reversed and scaled). For $e = 1$: reflection with equal angles (specular). For $e < 1$: the rebound is MORE GRAZING: $\tan\theta' = \tan\theta/e$ measured from the normal - the reflected angle exceeds the incident angle. Energy: $K_f/K_i = \sin^2\theta + e^2\cos^2\theta$.

cards.title: Fixed walls and inclines as 2-D collisions (cont.)
items: Smooth incline (angle $\alpha$ with horizontal): the line of impact is the incline normal; decompose along the normal and the incline; the normal component flips as $e$; the along-incline component is untouched. For a ball bouncing off a 30-degree incline elastically, the angle of departure is a pure geometry exercise: reflect the velocity across the normal (mirror rule) - the angle to the incline is preserved.

the wall is the $m_2 \to \infty$ limit of the two-sphere problem; the wall's velocity is what enters the restitution law ($v_{sep} = e\,v_{app}$ with the wall's motion included, CM-21). The finite-mass formulas degenerate cleanly: the wall never moves.

cards.title: Fixed walls and inclines as 2-D collisions (cont.)
items: energy check on wall rebound at 45 degrees, $e = 0.8$: $K_f/K_i = 0.5 + 0.64\times0.5 = 0.82$; direct: $(v\sin45)^2 + (0.8 v\cos45)^2 = v^2(0.5+0.32) = 0.82 v^2$.

cards.title: Equal masses, elastic, target at rest: the velocities separate at 90 d.
items: Theorem: if two equal-mass smooth spheres collide elastically and one is initially at rest, their velocity vectors after the collision are perpendicular: $\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90$ degrees (angles measured from the original direction). Proof in two lines: momentum $m\mathbf{u} = m\mathbf{v}_1 + m\mathbf{v}_2$ gives $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2$; elastic KE conservation gives $u^2 = v_1^2 + v_2^2$.

Dot the momentum result with itself: $u^2 = v_1^2 + v_2^2 + 2\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_2$. Comparing: $\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_2 = 0$ - perpendicular. Done. Note the masses cancel in the first equation because they are EQUAL - that is the whole scope condition.

cards.title: Equal masses, elastic, target at rest: the velocities separate at 90 d.

Worked (source E6): deflection $30$ degrees: $\theta_2 = 60$ degrees; $v_1 = u\cos30 = 0.866u$; $v_2 = u\sin30 = 0.5u$. Momentum-x:

cards.title: Equal masses, elastic, target at rest: the velocities separate at 90 d.
items: Scope and failure modes: (i) unequal masses: NOT 90 degrees - $\theta_1 + \theta_2 < 90$ degrees when $m_1 > m_2$, and the shooter's angle is capped at $\arcsin(m_2/m_1)$ (OLY-02); (ii) $e < 1$: KE drops, the dot-product step fails, the angle is NOT 90 degrees; (iii) rough spheres: tangential impulses change the perpendicular components; (iv) head-on ($\theta_1 = 0$): the shooter stops - the 1-D limit (CM-08).

the dot-product proof works because momentum conservation gives a VECTOR triangle and elasticity gives its SIDE LENGTHS: a right triangle is the only triangle with $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. Any violation of the theorem's conditions breaks one of those two inputs.

Any collision-then-motion problem splits into stages with DIFFERENT conservation laws. Stage 1 (the collision, duration milliseconds): momentum conserved (no external impulse); energy NOT conserved (deformation heat). Stage 2 (the motion afterwards: swing, slide, spring): energy conserved (smooth; only conservative forces); momentum NOT conserved (gravity/tension/spring force is external). The order is fixed:

cards.title: The two-stage protocol: momentum first, energy second (cont.)
items: never use energy across the collision, never use momentum across the swing. Write each stage's equation, then chain them through the shared velocity.

Ballistic pendulum (source E5): bullet mass $m$ at $v_0$ embeds in a hanging block $M$. Collision: $mv_0 = (m+M)V$, so $V = \dfrac{m v_0}{m+M}$. Swing: $\frac{1}{2}(m+M)V^2 = (m+M)gh$, so $V = \sqrt{2gh}$. Chain: $v_0 = \dfrac{m+M}{m}\sqrt{2gh}$.

cards.title: The two-stage protocol: momentum first, energy second (cont.)
items: Reverse problems: given $h$, find $v_0$: $V = \sqrt{2gh}$ then $v_0 = \frac{m+M}{m}V$. Source Q12: 5 g bullet, 1 kg block, $h = 0.1$ m: $V = \sqrt{2} = 1.414$ m/s; $v_0 = (1.005/0.005)(1.414) = 284$ m/s. Source P29: 10 g, 2 kg, $h = 0.05$ m: $V = 1$ m/s; $v_0 = (2.01/0.01)(1) = 201$ m/s;

cards.title: The two-stage protocol: momentum first, energy second (cont.)
items: energy lost in the collision: 202 J down to 1.005 J = 99.5% (stage 1 is violently inelastic).

the collision time is short so gravity's impulse $mg\Delta t$ is negligible - momentum is the right stage-1 law. The swing time is long and the forces are conservative - energy is the right stage-2 law. Mixing them (energy across the embed, momentum across the swing) is the classic examiner trap.

If it compresses a spring: $\frac{1}{2}Mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}kx_{max}^2$ (CM-14). The protocol generalises: stage 1 momentum; stage 2 energy with whichever conservative/resistive forces apply; sometimes a stage 3.

items: Trap: the ballistic-pendulum formula $v_0 = \frac{m+M}{m}\sqrt{2gh}$ ASSUMES the bullet stays in. If a problem says 'emerges', 'passes through', 'lodges and sticks with extra mass', rewrite stage 1 for that geometry. Same for a bullet that embeds but the block is on a spring (then stage 1 is momentum, stage 2 is spring energy: $\frac{1}{2}(m+M)V^2 = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$).
Q19 momentum audit with signs: bullet direction positive: $5 = 2 + v$; if the bullet had exited BACKWARD at 200: $5 = -2 + v$, $v = 7$ m/s - the sign convention matters more than the numbers.

cards.title: Energy fraction in the ballistic pendulum (the examiner favourite)
items: General fraction lost in stage 1: $1 - K_f/K_i = 1 - \frac{m}{m+M} = \frac{M}{m+M}$ (using $V = \frac{m}{m+M}v_0$: $K_f = \frac{1}{2}\frac{m^2 v_0^2}{m+M}$, so $K_f/K_i = \frac{m}{m+M}$). For $M \gg m$: nearly ALL the bullet's KE dies in the block - P29's 99.5%. The retained fraction $m/(m+M)$ keeps the pair moving; the rest is heat and deformation.

Stage 2 then loses nothing (smooth swing) but converts KE to PE. The height reached is $h = \frac{m^2 v_0^2}{2g(m+M)^2}$. For a given $h$, larger $M$ means larger $v_0$ measurement sensitivity - the practical ballistic pendulum: measure $h$, get $v_0$ with the factor $(m+M)/m$ (a 200x amplification for 10 g in 2 kg).

cards.title: The CM frame: where collisions become trivial
items: The CM (centre-of-mass) frame moves with $\mathbf{v}_{cm} = \dfrac{m_1\mathbf{u}_1 + m_2\mathbf{u}_2}{m_1+m_2}$. In that frame the total momentum is ZERO by construction: $m_1\mathbf{u}'_1 + m_2\mathbf{u}'_2 = 0$, so $\mathbf{u}'_2 = -\frac{m_1}{m_2}\mathbf{u}'_1$ - the two bodies always approach (or recede) along one line, equal and opposite momenta.
The frame is inertial before and after the collision (COM velocity changes only under external impulse) - so Newton's laws hold in it.

cards.title: The CM frame: where collisions become trivial (cont.)
items: Elastic collisions in the CM frame are TRIVIAL: the velocities simply reverse direction (speeds unchanged: $|\mathbf{u}'_i| = |\mathbf{v}'_i|$; directions flipped along the line of impact). Reason: momentum zero means the momenta reverse (any other outcome would need internal energy change); elasticity keeps the speeds.
In 2-D the reversal happens along the line of impact while the common rotation of both vectors by the scattering angle is free - the magnitude statement is $|v'_i| = |u'_i|$ with direction changed.

title: The CM frame: where collisions become trivial

cards.title: The CM frame: where collisions become trivial (cont.)

First term = the KE of the COM motion (untouchable); second = the KE of relative motion (the collision's play money). For $m_1 = m_2 = m$: $\mu = m/2$, $M = 2m$:

cards.title: The CM frame: where collisions become trivial (cont.)
items: why the decomposition is exact: $\sum \frac{1}{2}m_i v_i^2 = \frac{1}{2}M v_{cm}^2 + \frac{1}{2}\mu v_{rel}^2$ for two bodies is the parallel-axis theorem for kinetic energy - expand $\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{v}_{cm} + \mathbf{v}'_i$ and the cross terms vanish because $\sum m_i \mathbf{v}'_i = 0$.

source P36(a-b): derive the decomposition (done); CM KE is unchanged by the collision because momentum conservation leaves $v_{cm}$ fixed. The lab-frame velocities are just $\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{v}_{cm} + \mathbf{v}'_i$ - transform back and you have solved any collision by inspection.

cards.title: The CM-frame recipe for 2-D scattering
items: Recipe: (1) compute $\mathbf{v}_{cm}$ and the CM velocities $\mathbf{u}'_i = \mathbf{u}_i - \mathbf{v}_{cm}$; (2) in CM the collision reverses/rotates the velocities (elastic: reverse the relative velocity along the line of impact; keep magnitudes); (3) transform back $\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{v}_{cm} + \mathbf{v}'_i$. For a target at rest, $u'_1 = \frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}u$, $u'_2 = -\frac{m_1}{m_1+m_2}u$ - approach speeds in CM are INVERSELY mass-weighted.

cards.title: The CM-frame recipe for 2-D scattering (cont.)
items: The equal-mass 90-degree rule (CM-12) is one line in this language: $\mathbf{v}_{cm} = \mathbf{u}/2$; after reversal $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{u}/2 + \mathbf{w}$, $\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{u}/2 - \mathbf{w}$ with $|\mathbf{w}| = u/2$ (speeds in CM preserved); $\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_2 = u^2/4 - w^2 = 0$ perpendicular. ANY elastic equal-mass collision with a resting target lands on this circle of radius $u/2$ around $\mathbf{u}/2$ - the locus of possible exit velocities is a circle (useful for maximum/minimum questions!).

title: The CM frame: where collisions become trivial (cont.)

takeaway: K = 1/2 M v_cm^2 + 1/2 mu v_rel^2; in the CM frame elastic collisions just reverse velocities.

cards.title: The CM-frame recipe for 2-D scattering (cont.)
items: Max-deflection questions: the shooter's exit velocity $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{v}_{cm} + \mathbf{v}'_1$ is the sum of a fixed vector and a vector of fixed length $\frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}u$ at variable angle. The extreme directions are tangent to that circle - this gives the maximum scattering angle (the OLY-02 formula $\theta_{max} = \arcsin(m_2/m_1)$ for $m_1 > m_2$ in one geometric picture).

cards.title: CM language for explosions and multi-body problems
items: work E6 in CM: $u = v_0$ along $x$; $v_{cm} = v_0/2$; CM speeds $v_0/2$ each. Shooter deflected 30 in lab at speed $0.866 v_0$: $\mathbf{v}_1 = (0.75, 0.433)v_0$; $\mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_{cm} = (0.25, 0.433)v_0$ with length $0.5 v_0$ matches CM speed. Target: $\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_{cm} + \mathbf{v}'_2 = (0.5,0) + (-0.25, -0.433) = (0.25, -0.433)v_0$; length $= 0.5 v_0$ - both CM speeds preserved.

Explosion: all fragments' momenta sum to $M\mathbf{v}_{cm}$; in the CM frame they scatter with zero total momentum. For three equal masses: momentum triangle closes (CM-03). For n fragments, the CM frame is where you compute the minimum/maximum possible speed of one fragment: e.g. two fragments fly off with momenta $\mathbf{p}, -\mathbf{p}$ in CM; lab speeds span $|v_{cm} \pm p/m|$.

cards.title: CM language for explosions and multi-body problems (cont.)
items: Collisions of more than two bodies: pairwise with $e$ bookkeeping; the CM frame of the PAIR is the natural frame per contact. A ball bouncing between two moving walls: use the wall's frame for each bounce (CM-21), then compose velocities.

the relativistic generalisation keeps the same structure: $K = \gamma_{cm}Mc^2 + K_{rel}$; the CM frame is still where total momentum vanishes. The non-relativistic decomposition suffices for JEE/Olympiad classical problems.

cards.title: CM language for explosions and multi-body problems (cont.)
items: invariant audit: $v_{cm}$ is the same before and after any internal rearrangement; $K_{cm}$ likewise. If a computation changes $K_{cm}$, the momentum bookkeeping is wrong.

title: The CM frame: where collisions become trivial (cont.)
subtitle: CM frame definition; velocity reversal for elastic; energy decomposition; circle locus; drills.
takeaway: K = 1/2 M v_cm^2 + 1/2 mu v_rel^2; in the CM frame elastic collisions just reverse velocities.

cards.title: CM-frame drills (cont.)
items: (b) Explosion of 4 kg at 10 m/s into 1 kg and 3 kg: $v_{cm} = 10$; CM momenta $\pm p$; lab speeds $10 \pm p/m$. If the 1 kg piece gets $v = 13$ in lab: $p = 1(3) = 3$; 3 kg piece: $10 - 1 = 9$ m/s.

cards.title: Picking mass up and throwing it down: F = m_dot v
items: A conveyor belt runs at speed $v$; sand falls on it at rate $\dot m$ (kg/s) with zero horizontal velocity. To carry the sand, the belt must deliver to each kilogram the momentum $v$: force $F = \dot m v$. Worked (source E7): $\dot m = 5$ kg/s, $v = 2$ m/s: $F = 10$ N. Power delivered by the motor: $P = Fv = \dot m v^2 = 20$ W. But the sand's KE grows at only $\frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2 = 10$ W.
The missing 10 W is heat - friction between sand and belt scatters the KE as the grains slide to rest in the belt frame.

cards.title: Picking mass up and throwing it down: F = m_dot v (cont.)
items: The factor-2 is universal for inelastic pickup from rest: belt power $= \dot m v^2$, KE rate $= \frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2$, heat rate $= \frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2$. Examiners love the 'where does the other half go' question (source E7/P34): answer: sliding friction heat at the pickup (and if the sand is thrown OFF the belt at the far end, that KE is carried away with the sand - different audit!).

cards.title: Picking mass up and throwing it down: F = m_dot v (cont.)
items: Cart collecting sand (OLY-10): a cart of mass $M$ rolling at $v$ on a smooth floor collects rain/sand falling vertically at $\dot m$: horizontal momentum is conserved (vertical rain has none), so $Mv = (M + \dot m t)v(t)$: $v(t) = \dfrac{M v_0}{M + \dot m t}$ - the cart slows. A cart that LEAKS sand vertically:

subtitle: F = m_dot v; belt power split; cart pickup and leak; sign discipline; drills.

takeaway: Picking mass up or throwing it down needs force m_dot v; belt power splits half KE, half heat.

cards.title: Picking mass up and throwing it down: F = m_dot v (cont.)
items: $v$ constant (the dropped sand takes its own momentum); a cart REJECTED from a hopper at speed $u$ rel needs thrust $\dot m(u - v)$ - sign bookkeeping always via momentum of (cart + ejected mass) per $dt$.

the pickup force is momentum flux: mass $\dot m$ per second crosses from speed 0 to speed $v$; the momentum source is the belt, paid as $\dot m v$. Same law as the rocket (CM-17) and the falling chain (OLY-01) with different geometries.
P34(a): $\dot m = 3$ kg/s at $v = 4$ m/s: $F = 12$ N, $P = 48$ W, KE rate $= 24$ W, heat $= 24$ W - exactly the factor-2 split.

cards.title: Sand thrown off: the full belt audit
items: If sand lands at rest and leaves the belt at speed $v$ (belt length $L$, speed $v$): power in $\dot m v^2$; KE out $\frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2$ carried away; heat $\frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2$. If instead the belt STOPS the sand (sand lands moving at $v$ and the belt brings it to rest): force $= \dot m v$ still, but now the KE $\frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2$ is destroyed entirely - all heat.
The audit table depends on in/out speeds; the momentum flux law $F = \dot m (v_{out} - v_{in})$ never changes.

cards.title: Sand thrown off: the full belt audit (cont.)
items: Hopper onto a cart: $F = \dot m u$ if the cart must accelerate the sand from rest to its own speed $u$; the cart's engine force $F$ at speed $u$ delivers $P = \dot m u^2$ of which half is KE rate - only if the sand starts at rest in the lab. If the sand is thrown forward at $w$ relative to the cart: thrust bookkeeping via the rocket sign discipline (CM-17): the safest exam route is to write momentum of the whole system at $t$ and $t+dt$ and expand.

cart collecting rain at 0.1 kg/s from 5 m/s at $t = 0$, $M = 20$ kg: at $t = 100$ s: $v = 100/30 = 3.33$ m/s; KE: 250 J to $\frac{1}{2}(30)(11.1) = 166.7$ J; the 83.3 J lost is the pickup heat, matching the differential identity $\frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2 = -\frac{d}{dt}KE$.

cards.title: Sand thrown off: the full belt audit (cont.)
items: the sand-on-belt P = 2 x KE-rate result reappears in fluid jets (OLY-07: F = rho A v^2 on a plate) and the falling chain (OLY-01: flux 2 lambda g x) - one momentum-flux law, many costumes.

The universal recipe: system = (body + the mass being exchanged) over $dt$; write $p(t)$ and $p(t+dt)$; keep every term to FIRST order in $dt$; drop products like $dm\,dv$. The force on the body: $F_{on\,body} = \dot m_{in} u_{in} - \dot m_{out} u_{out}$ (momentum brought in minus carried out) plus external forces. For the rocket:
$m\,dv = -v_e\,dm$ with $dm < 0$ (mass lost) - signs set by the exhaust velocity RELATIVE to the body.
