cards.title: Variable-mass sign discipline (cont.)
items: Traps: (1) using the sand's speed instead of the RELATIVE speed for rockets (CM-17); (2) forgetting the sand carries momentum away when it leaves a cart (that IS the retarding force on leaky carts); (3) assuming energy conservation anywhere in these problems - variable-mass pickup is dissipative by nature.

leaky cart: $M$ moving at $v$ leaks at $\dot m$ vertically down. Horizontal momentum of cart: the leaked grains keep horizontal speed $v$; the leak takes $\dot m v$ per second but the cart's remaining momentum per mass stays: $\dot v = 0$ - $v$ CONSTANT (the classic result: leaking does not slow the cart; loading does).

cards.title: Drills: flux and belt
items: (a) Belt 1.5 m/s, sand 2 kg/s: $F = 3$ N, $P = 4.5$ W, KE rate 2.25 W. (b) Rain 0.02 kg/s into a 100 kg cart at 2 m/s: $F = 0.04$ N retarding at first; after 100 s the cart holds 2 kg of water and moves $200/102 = 1.96$ m/s. (c) Water jet 3 kg/s at 8 m/s onto a wall (stops): $F = 24$ N (OLY-07).

(d) Belt problem with friction coefficient given: if the question gives $\mu$ between sand and belt, the static friction force on the sand is $\dot m v$ total; belt tension difference equals it - solve as a friction-engineering problem, not a collision.

cards.title: Drills: flux and belt (cont.)
items: drill (b): momentum 200 kg m/s conserved; total mass 102; $v = 1.9608$; KE: initial 200 J; final $\frac{1}{2}(102)(3.845) = 196.1$ J; lost 3.9 J = pickup heat.

Derivation in the lab frame (source 3.9-3.10): rocket mass $m$, speed $v$; in time $dt$ it ejects mass $-dm > 0$ at exhaust speed $v_e$ RELATIVE to the rocket (backward), so exhaust lab speed $= v - v_e$. Momentum conservation for rocket + exhaust (no external impulse): $mv = (m + dm)(v + dv) + (-dm)(v - v_e)$. Expand:

cards.title: Delta v = v_e ln(m0/m_f): the rocket equation (cont.)
items: $mv = mv + m\,dv + v\,dm + dm\,dv - v\,dm + v_e\,dm$; cancel and drop the second-order $dm\,dv$: $m\,dv + v_e\,dm = 0$, so $dv = -v_e\,dm/m$. Integrate from $m_0$ to $m_f$: $\Delta v = v_e \ln\dfrac{m_0}{m_f}$.

Reading the formula: $\Delta v$ depends on the exhaust speed and the MASS RATIO only - not on the burn rate, not on the time profile. Gravity-free, drag-free, constant $v_e$ - those are the assumptions (state them). With gravity acting upward during vertical climb: $dv = -v_e dm/m - g\,dt$ and the integral gains $-g t_{burn}$. Thrust:

title: Delta v = v_e ln(m0/m_f): the rocket equation
subtitle: Rocket equation derivation; thrust; assumptions; multi-burn and drills.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. 3.10 / E10 Q25; independently checked
takeaway: Rocket: delta v = v_e ln(m0/m_f); thrust = m_dot v_e; the exhaust momentum is the point, not the pushed air.

cards.title: Delta v = v_e ln(m0/m_f): the rocket equation (cont.)
items: $F = \dot m v_e$ with $\dot m = |dm/dt|$ (source Q25: $\dot m = 2$ kg/s at 3000 m/s: $F = 6000$ N).

Numbers (source E10): $v_e = 3$ km/s, $m_0/m_f = 10$: $\Delta v = 3\ln 10 = 3(2.303) = 6.91$ km/s - orbit-class. Source Q8: need $\Delta v = 4$ km/s with $v_e = 2$ km/s: $m_0/m_f = e^{2} = 7.39$. Source P24: $v_e = 2500$, $\Delta v = 5000$: $m_0/m_f = e^2 = 7.39$. Note the answer to 'how much fuel' is EXPONENTIAL in the mission $\Delta v$ - the tyranny of the rocket equation.

why no air is needed: the rocket pushes on its own exhaust, not on the atmosphere. Source P16: rockets work in vacuum. The momentum ledger is closed: every bit of forward momentum of the rocket is paid by backward exhaust momentum.

cards.title: Delta v = v_e ln(m0/m_f): the rocket equation (cont.)
items: the limit $m_0/m_f = e$ gives $\Delta v = v_e$ (about 63% of the launch mass is propellant); $m_f \to m_0$ (no fuel) gives $\Delta v = 0$; doubling $m_0/m_f$ adds $v_e \ln 2 \approx 0.69 v_e$ - logarithmic, not linear.

Thrust $F = \dot m v_e$ is independent of rocket speed (in the rocket's frame the exhaust leaves at $v_e$ regardless). Power delivered to the ROCKET: $P = Fv = \dot m v_e v$ (speed-dependent!); the exhaust KE rate is $\frac{1}{2}\dot m v_e^2$ - both are frame-dependent bookkeeping; the invariant statement is momentum flux.
In the instantaneous rest frame of the rocket, the exhaust carries away KE $\frac{1}{2}\dot m v_e^2$ in that frame.

cards.title: Thrust and power; the burn-rate freedom (cont.)
items: Multi-burn problems: apply $\Delta v = v_e \ln(m_{start}/m_{end})$ per stage/burn and ADD the $\Delta v$s (they are speed increments along the path; for collinear burns). Two-stage rockets (OLY-06): the real gain is dropping dead structure; with ZERO structural mass any split gives the same $\Delta v = v_e \ln(M/M_p)$.
with gravity: $\Delta v = v_e \ln(m_0/m_f) - g t_b$ for a vertical burn of duration $t_b$; the gravity loss is why real launches turn downrange quickly.
Q25 audit: thrust 6000 N on 1000 kg initial gives $a = 6$ m/s$^2$ at burn start - half a g; the mass falls as fuel burns so acceleration grows. Sign check: $dm < 0$; $-v_e dm/m > 0$ speeds up.

cards.title: The variable-mass ledger for exams
items: Choose system: rocket + exhaust (closed). Write momentum at $t$ and $t + dt$. Keep first order. Integrate. Assumptions to state: (1) $v_e$ constant relative to the rocket; (2) exhaust collinear; (3) no external impulse (or add $g$ term); (4) all mass ejected is propellant. The same ledger solves sprinklers (water leaving a cart), sand hoppers (CM-16) and jetpacks.

Sprinkler-on-a-cart: cart mass $M$ (with water), ejects at $\dot m$ at $v_e$ rel: same equation $M dv = v_e (-dM)$ if no external force; the cart accelerates like a rocket until the water runs out. Fire-extinguisher recoil: treat the spray as exhaust with $v_e$ = spray speed relative to the cylinder.

title: Delta v = v_e ln(m0/m_f): the rocket equation (cont.)
subtitle: Rocket equation derivation; thrust; assumptions; multi-burn and drills.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. 3.10 / E10 Q25; independently checked
takeaway: Rocket: delta v = v_e ln(m0/m_f); thrust = m_dot v_e; the exhaust momentum is the point, not the pushed air.

cards.title: The variable-mass ledger for exams (cont.)
items: the rocket equation is just $F = dp/dt$ for a system with flowing mass: $p = mv$ differentiates to $m\,dv + v\,dm$; the exhaust takes the $v\,dm$ term away at speed $v - v_e$ so the leftover is $m\,dv + v_e\,dm = 0$.
extinction case: $m_f = m_0/2$: $\Delta v = v_e \ln 2 = 0.69 v_e$; half the mass as fuel gives only 0.69 exhaust-speeds - the classic 'rockets are inefficient' table entry.

cards.title: Rocket drills
items: (a) $v_e = 2$ km/s, fuel 80% of mass: $m_0/m_f = 5$: $\Delta v = 2\ln 5 = 3.22$ km/s. (b) Need 9 km/s with $v_e = 3$: $m_0/m_f = e^3 = 20.1$ - 95% fuel. (c) Thrust 20 kN at $\dot m = 50$ kg/s: $v_e = 400$ m/s. (d) A 5 kg cart with a 2 kg spring-loaded mass shot at 6 m/s rel: cart + remaining 3 kg at $v$; ejected 2 kg at $v - 6$; momentum: $0 = 3v + 2(v-6) = 5v - 12$; $v = 2.4$ m/s.
drill (d) energy: cart KE $= \frac{1}{2}(3)(5.76) = 8.64$ J; ejecta KE $= \frac{1}{2}(2)(3.6^2) = 12.96$ J; total 21.6 J from the spring. Momentum $= 7.2 - 7.2 = 0$.

cards.title: Chains and jets: momentum flux is m_dot v on top of the carried w.
items: Chain lifted at constant speed $v$ from a pile on the ground (source P34c, Q13 family): at the moment a length $x$ hangs clear, the force at the top must (1) support the hanging weight $\lambda x g$ and (2) supply the momentum flux to jerk each stationary link up to speed $v$: $F = \lambda x g + \lambda v^2$ with $\lambda = M/L$. P34(c) with $M = 2$ kg, $v = 3$ m/s, $g = 10$: $F = (2/L)(10x + 9)$ N.
The source's Q13 (mass 3 kg at 2 m/s) is under-specified without $L$ or $x$ - the general formula is the answer (recorded in SOURCE-AUDIT).

cards.title: Chains and jets: momentum flux is m_dot v on top of the carried w.
items: Energetics of the lift (the exam's 'where does the work go'): power delivered $P = Fv = \lambda x g v + \lambda v^3$. Rate of PE growth $= \frac{d}{dt}(\frac{1}{2}\lambda x^2 g) = \lambda x g v$ matches the weight term. Rate of KE growth $= \frac{d}{dt}(\frac{1}{2}\lambda x v^2) = \frac{1}{2}\lambda v^3$. So HALF the flux work $\lambda v^3$ becomes KE and HALF is dissipated jerking the links from rest to $v$ at the pickup (inelastic).

The pile itself does no work: pickup happens at zero displacement - the chain links at rest are accelerated by tension acting over vanishing displacement; the energy audit closes only with the pickup heat included.

title: Chains and jets: momentum flux is m_dot v on top of the carried weight
subtitle: Flux law F = m_dot v; chain lift with pickup heat; jets; drills and classification.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. 3.10 / Q13 P34 OL9; independently checked
takeaway: Momentum flux: F = m_dot v = lambda v^2 on top of the carried weight; jets push rho A v^2.

cards.title: Chains and jets: momentum flux is m_dot v on top of the carried w.
items: Water jet on a fixed plate (OLY-07, source OL9): jet speed $v$, area $A$, density $\rho$: mass rate $\dot m = \rho A v$; the horizontal momentum is destroyed (splatters sideways): $F = \dot m v = \rho A v^2$. At angle $\theta$ to the plate surface: only the normal component $v\sin\theta$ dies: $F_n = \rho A v^2 \sin\theta$. Moving plate at $u$ (same direction as jet): relative speed $v - u$:
$F = \rho A (v-u)^2$ - the flux law always uses relative speed (details in OLY-07).

cards.title: Chains and jets: momentum flux is m_dot v on top of the carried w.
items: one law: $F = \frac{dp}{dt} = \dot m \Delta v$. When mass arrives at rest and is carried at $v$: $\Delta v = v$; when a jet dies on a plate: $\Delta v = v$; when a chain is jerked: $\Delta v = v$; when a rocket ejects: $\Delta v = v_e$. Every flux problem is this multiplication with a diagram.
jet numbers: $A = 5$ cm$^2$, $v = 20$ m/s, $\rho = 1000$: $\dot m = 10$ kg/s, $F = 200$ N - about 20 kg-weight, a fire-hose kick.

cards.title: Chains and jets: momentum flux is m_dot v on top of the carried w.
items: A chain segment lands and stops: the flux force stopping it is $\lambda v^2$ where $v$ is the landing speed. If the segment falls a distance $x$: $v^2 = 2gx$, flux force $= 2\lambda g x$; plus the landed weight $\lambda x g$ gives a total $3\lambda x g$ - the classic result: the scale reads THREE times the landed weight at every instant, ending at $3mg$ when the last link lands.
The chain-lift flux $\lambda v^2$ is the same term seen from above (OLY-01 does the full derivation and the variant geometry).

cards.title: Chain landing on a scale (preview of OLY-01) (cont.)
items: Exam phrasings to recognise: 'a uniform chain of linear density $\lambda$ falls onto a scale' vs 'is lifted from a pile at constant speed' vs 'hangs over a smooth peg' (OLY-05) - three geometries, one flux law plus one weight law.
the inelastic pickup/landing heat is exactly $\frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2$ at every link - the same half-half split as the belt (CM-16).
dimension: $\lambda v^2 = $ kg/m $\times$ m$^2$/s$^2$ = kg m/s$^2$ = N; $\lambda x g$ = kg/m $\times$ m $\times$ m/s$^2$ = N. Both terms are forces, adding is legitimate.

title: Chains and jets: momentum flux is m_dot v on top of the carried weight (cont.)
subtitle: Flux law F = m_dot v; chain lift with pickup heat; jets; drills and classification.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. 3.10 / Q13 P34 OL9; independently checked
takeaway: Momentum flux: F = m_dot v = lambda v^2 on top of the carried weight; jets push rho A v^2.

cards.title: Chain-lift and jet drills
items: (a) Chain 4 kg, 2 m long, lifted at constant 3 m/s: when 1.2 m is clear: $F = 2(1.2)(10) + 2(9) = 24 + 18 = 42$ N. (b) Jet $\rho = 1000$ kg/m$^3$, $A = 3$ cm$^2$, $v = 15$ m/s on a wall: $F = \rho A v^2 = 1000(3\times10^{-4})(225) = 67.5$ N. (c) Jet at 60 degrees to a plate surface:
$F_n = \rho A v^2 \sin 60 = 0.866\,\rho A v^2$; at 30 degrees to the surface: $0.5\,\rho A v^2$ - the angle is measured to the SURFACE so that the normal component is $v\sin\theta$.

cards.title: Chain-lift and jet drills (cont.)
items: (d) Belt at 4 m/s with 6 kg/s sand from rest: $F = 24$ N; $P = 96$ W; KE rate 48 W; heat 48 W (CM-16 again). (e) Chain falling onto a scale: reading $= 3\lambda x g$ at landed length $x$ (OLY-01).

drill (a): $\lambda = 2$; $F = \lambda x g + \lambda v^2 = 24 + 18 = 42$ N. Drill (b): $\dot m = \rho A v = 1000(3\times10^{-4})(15) = 4.5$ kg/s; $F = \dot m v = 4.5\times15 = 67.5$ N - the $\rho A v^2$ form and the $\dot m v$ form agree exactly.

cards.title: Which flux problem is which
items: Classification table. Chain lifted: weight + flux; half the flux work heats the pickup. Chain landing: landed weight + flux; reading up to 3x weight. Jet on plate: pure flux $\rho A v^2$; on a moving plate use relative speed. Belt pickup: flux $\dot m v$; belt power $\dot m v^2$. Rocket: flux $\dot m v_e$ = thrust. Rain into cart: retarding flux.
In every case draw the control volume first - what crosses the boundary, at what velocity - then write $\dot m \Delta v$.

cards.title: Which flux problem is which (cont.)
items: the control-volume picture is what the fluid-mechanics chapter will formalise as the momentum equation; here it is Newton's second law with a flow diagram.

re-derive the universal form: mass $dm$ crosses with velocity $u_{in}$ and leaves/absorbs at $u_{out}$; force $= \frac{dm}{dt}(u_{out} - u_{in})$ - every entry in the table is this with substituted speeds.

title: Man on a boat: the COM stays fixed, the parts slide apart
subtitle: Man on boat and block on wedge; COM-fixed displacements; drills.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. 3.12 / E8 Q10; independently checked
takeaway: Man on boat: horizontal COM fixed; ground displacement = M d/(m + M) opposite to the walk.

cards.title: Man on a boat: the COM stays fixed, the parts slide apart
items: System: man ($m$) + boat ($M$), initially at rest on frictionless water. No external horizontal force, so the horizontal COM stays FIXED: $m x_m + M x_b = $ const. If the man walks a distance $d$ RELATIVE to the boat, then $x_m - x_b = d + $ const and the ground displacements satisfy $m s_m + M s_b = 0$ with $s_m - s_b = d$. Solve:
$s_m = \dfrac{M d}{m+M}$ (man's ground displacement), $s_b = -\dfrac{m d}{m+M}$ (boat slides the other way).

cards.title: Man on a boat: the COM stays fixed, the parts slide apart (cont.)
items: Worked (source E8): 60 kg man walks 3 m on a 120 kg boat: $s_m = 120(3)/180 = 2$ m forward; $s_b = -60(3)/180 = -1$ m: the boat moves 1 m opposite. Total check: $60(2) + 120(-1) = 0$ (COM fixed); $s_m + |s_b| = 3 = d$ (the relative walk fully accounted for). Source Q10: 60 kg person JUMPS at 3 m/s relative to the boat:
momentum $0 = 60(3 + v_b) + 120 v_b$ (person lab speed $= 3 + v_b$): $180 + 180 v_b = 0$, $v_b = -1$ m/s - the boat recoils at 1 m/s.

cards.title: Man on a boat: the COM stays fixed, the parts slide apart (cont.)
items: Traps: (1) confusing ground displacement with relative displacement - $s_m = Md/(m+M)$ assumes $d$ is measured relative TO THE BOAT; (2) the boat's displacement is opposite; (3) total momentum is zero but the parts' momenta are not; (4) if the water is NOT frictionless, external horizontal friction moves the COM and the fixed-COM shortcut dies.

the COM line stays vertical-fixed because no horizontal external force acts; every internal shuffle trades equal opposite momenta: $m v_m = -M v_b$ at every instant; integrate and the displacements follow.

cards.title: Block on a movable wedge - the same COM law in 2-D
items: source P20: all three statements true: COM fixed; boat opposite; man ground displacement $Md/(m+M)$ with $d$ relative to the boat.

Block ($m$) slides down a movable wedge ($M$) on a smooth table: horizontal momentum of block\wedge is conserved (gravity and the table normal are vertical; the block-wedge normal pair is internal). The horizontal COM stays fixed: as the block descends and moves right relative to the wedge, the wedge slides left so that $m x_b + M x_w = $ const.
Vertical momentum is NOT conserved (the floor's normal force and gravity do not cancel).

title: Man on a boat: the COM stays fixed, the parts slide apart (cont.)
subtitle: Man on boat and block on wedge; COM-fixed displacements; drills.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. 3.12 / E8 Q10; independently checked
takeaway: Man on boat: horizontal COM fixed; ground displacement = M d/(m + M) opposite to the walk.

cards.title: Block on a movable wedge - the same COM law in 2-D (cont.)
items: Constraint version: if the block slides a relative horizontal distance $s_{rel}$ along the wedge: $s_{block} = \frac{M}{m+M}s_{rel}$, $s_{wedge} = -\frac{m}{m+M}s_{rel}$ - the same formula as the boat. The geometry is identical whenever horizontal external impulse is zero. For a wedge of incline angle $\alpha$ and slide length $L$ along the incline: $s_{rel} = L\cos\alpha$.

Energy: for the wedge problem energy IS conserved (smooth): $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv_b^2 + \frac{1}{2}Mv_w^2$ with the constraint $v_{bx} = v_{wx} + v_{rel\,x}$ - a two-equation solve. For the boat walk energy is NOT conserved (muscles); use momentum/COM only. The wedge problem is the standard 'both conservation laws, different stages' exam question.

cards.title: Block on a movable wedge - the same COM law in 2-D (cont.)
items: mass-ratio sanity: $M \gg m$: the wedge barely moves and the block does almost all the sliding; $m \gg M$: the block barely moves and the wedge does almost all the sliding. Both limits pass through the same formula.

(a) 80 kg woman walks 4 m on a 40 kg raft: $s_{raft} = -80(4)/120 = -2.67$ m; $s_{woman} = 1.33$ m. A ball dropped from $h_1$ rebounds to $h_2$ on a fixed floor: impact speed $v = \sqrt{2gh_1}$, rebound speed $ev$, so $h_2 = e^2 h_1$ and $e = \sqrt{h_2/h_1}$. Source Q5: dropped from 5 m, bounces to 3.2 m: $e = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.8$. Source P10: rebounds to 64%: $e = 0.8$ again.
The height ratio is $e^2$, never $e$ - the classic trap (drop height 4 m, $e = 0.5$: rebound 1 m, not 2 m).

cards.title: Bounce heights: e = sqrt(h2/h1) and the geometric ladder (cont.)
items: Successive bounces (source P25/OL4): $h_n = e^{2n} h_0$ after $n$ bounces. $e = 0.7$ from 10 m: $h_3 = 10(0.7)^6 = 10(0.1176) = 1.176$ m. The heights form a geometric sequence with ratio $e^2$; the velocities with ratio $e$; the bounce times with ratio $e$ (since $t = \sqrt{2h/g} \propto e^n$).

cards.title: Bounce heights: e = sqrt(h2/h1) and the geometric ladder (cont.)
items: The two series differ (heights decay by $e^2$, times by $e$) - memorise which is which.

each bounce is a floor collision with $e$ defined on speeds; $h \propto v^2$ turns the speed ratio $e$ into the height ratio $e^2$. The geometric series follow because the process is self-similar: every bounce reproduces the previous one scaled.

P31(b): how many bounces until $h_n < 0.1$ m from 5 m with $e = 0.6$: $5(0.36)^n < 0.1$, $0.36^n < 0.02$, $n > \ln(0.02)/\ln(0.36) = 3.83$: so after 4 bounces ($h_4 = 5(0.36)^4 = 0.084$ m). The source's printed answer '5' used $|\ln 0.01|$ by mistake; 4 suffices (recorded in SOURCE-AUDIT).

cards.title: Series sums and the energy ladder
items: Energy after $n$ bounces: $E_n/E_0 = h_n/h_0 = e^{2n}$. The energy ladder decays by $e^2$ per bounce; total energy dissipated to the floor over infinite bounces $= E_0$ (everything eventually). For $e = 0.8$, after 5 bounces: $0.8^{10} = 0.107$ - about 11% of the original energy remains (source OL4).

Distance sum traps: (i) the FIRST drop counts once ($h$, not $2h$); (ii) each later height counts twice (up and down); (iii) if the ball is thrown DOWN initially, the first impact speed is larger: $v = \sqrt{v_0^2 + 2gh}$ and the first rebound height is $e^2(v_0^2+2gh)/2g$. Time sums similar: first drop $t_0$ once, later flights $2 t_0 e^k$.

cards.title: Bouncing-ball question types (cont.)
items: self-consistency: from $h_1, h_2$ alone compute both $e$ and the ratio $h_3 = e^2 h_2$; if a problem gives three heights, they must satisfy $h_2^2 = h_1 h_3$ (geometric middle) - e.g. Q23's 10, 6.4, 4.1: $6.4^2 = 40.96$ vs $10\times4.1 = 41$ (rounding: $e = 0.8$ exactly gives 4.096).

A wall moves at speed $v_w$; a ball with velocity $v_{before}$ (signed, same axis) bounces with restitution $e$ measured in RELATIVE speeds: $v_{after} - v_w = -e(v_{before} - v_w)$. Solve: $v_{after} = v_w - e(v_{before} - v_w)$. In the wall's frame it is an ordinary bounce (relative velocity reverses, scaled by $e$); transform back by adding $v_w$.

cards.title: Bouncing off a MOVING wall: the wall's speed enters the restitution.
items: Worked (source E9, with the source's own check-block error corrected): ball at 10 m/s toward a wall coming toward it at 5 m/s, $e = 0.8$. Take the ball's direction positive: $v_{before} = +10$, $v_w = -5$. Relative approach: $10 - (-5) = 15$ m/s. $v_{after} = -5 - 0.8(15) = -17$ m/s:

the ball rebounds at 17 m/s - FASTER than it came in, because the wall's KE paid the difference. The source's 'Check' block says 7 m/s (a sign slip: it used $v_{after} - v_w = +12$ instead of $-12$); the source's own solution block reaches the correct 17 m/s. Recorded in SOURCE-AUDIT.

cards.title: Bouncing off a MOVING wall: the wall's speed enters the restitution.
items: Source Q14: 1 kg ball at 3 m/s toward a wall moving toward it at 2 m/s, $e = 0.5$: $v_{after} = -2 - 0.5(5) = -4.5$ m/s: rebounds at 4.5 m/s. General lesson: a wall approaching at $u$ adds roughly $(1+e)u$ to the rebound speed; a receding wall subtracts it. Superball limit ($e = 1$, wall speed $u$ toward a ball at $v$): rebound $= v + 2u$ - the famous 'bounce off a moving train' boost.

restitution measures the relative speed of separation over approach AT THE CONTACT. The wall's motion changes both. Applying $e$ to lab speeds is the classic error - the formula $v_{after} - v_w = -e(v_{before} - v_w)$ encodes the frame change in one line.

A ball bounces on a vertically moving platform (full resonance story in OLY-04). One bounce, up-positive: ball at $v_{before}$ (negative if falling), platform at $v_w$ (positive if rising): $v_{after} = v_w - e(v_{before} - v_w) = (1+e)v_w - e v_{before}$. Platform rising at $u$ meets ball falling at speed $v$:

cards.title: Moving platform (the energy-pump machine) (cont.)
items: $v_{after} = (1+e)u + e v$ upward - larger than the fixed-floor rebound $ev$: the platform pumped $(1+e)u$ into the ball in one bounce.

Receding platform (falling away at $u$): the rebound weakens the same way. The invariant recipe: relative speeds in the $e$ law, then transform back; never apply $e$ to lab speeds when the surface moves. Elastic platform limit ($e = 1$, rising at $u$): $v_{after} = 2u + v$ - the ball leaves with its own speed plus twice the platform's.

limit $v_w = 0$: reduces to the fixed-floor law $v_{after} = -e v_{before}$. Elastic head-on ball vs rising platform: relative approach $v + u$; relative separation $v + u$; lab $= (v+u) + u = v + 2u$ - superelastic; platform energy transferred.

cards.title: Wall-collision drills
items: (a) Ball at 12 m/s hits a wall receding at 3 m/s (same direction as the ball), $e = 0.9$: $v_{after} = 3 - 0.9(12-3) = 3 - 8.1 = -5.1$ m/s: rebounds at 5.1 m/s - the receding wall 'stole' speed. (b) Ball at 8 m/s meets a wall coming at 6 m/s, $e = 1$: $v_{after} = -6 - 1(8+6) = -20$ m/s: rebounds at 20 m/s.

(c) Ball dropped 1.25 m ($v_{before} = -5$ m/s) onto a platform rising at +2 m/s, $e = 0.5$: $v_{after} = 2 - 0.5(-5-2) = 2 + 3.5 = 5.5$ m/s upward - use the formula with signed inputs, not ad-hoc speed arithmetic.

cards.title: Wall-collision drills (cont.)
items: drill (c) energy audit: ball KE in $= \frac{1}{2}m(25)$; out $= \frac{1}{2}m(30.25)$ - the ball gained, the rising platform did work. Drill (b): 32 J to 200 J for 1 kg - the moving wall paid.

A ball bouncing between two walls (one or both moving): apply $v' = v_w - e(v - v_w)$ per contact, alternating walls. Between two walls approaching at $u$ each (ball speed $v$ in lab): each bounce adds roughly $(1+e)u$ - the ball heats up like a gas piston; between two receding walls it cools. The wall-frame composition is the olympiad 'bouncing ball in a closing gap' family (OLY-04's fixed-platform cousin).

cards.title: The ten examiner traps, sharpened
items: (1) Energy conservation across an INELASTIC collision - never; use momentum (and $e$ if given). (2) Applying $e$ to the full velocity - $e$ lives only along the line of impact; tangential components are untouched for smooth bodies. (3) Forgetting the exhaust momentum in rocket problems - the rocket equation IS the exhaust ledger. (4) Using $v_{cm}$ as the velocity of every part after impact - only stuck parts share $v_{cm}$; separated parts do not.
(5) Mixing system and particle laws - $M a_{cm} = F_{ext}$ for the system, $F = ma$ for each piece.

cards.title: The ten examiner traps, sharpened (cont.)
items: (6) Assuming the COM stays fixed when external forces act - fixed only when $\int F_{ext} dt = 0$ in that direction. (7) Confusing impulse (N s) with force (N) - $J = \bar F \Delta t$. (8) Forgetting momentum is a vector - components conserve independently. (9) 'Heavy ball bounces back' - no: the heavy plows on, the light flies at nearly $2u_1 - u_2$.
(10) Using the ballistic-pendulum formula when the bullet EXITS - that formula assumes embedding ($e = 0$).
every trap is a broken conservation statement or a broken scope condition. The pre-submission audit (CM-23) checks exactly these.

cards.title: Trap 11 (source C9, corrected): equal bounce angles are NOT free
items: Source C9 asks: a ball hits a wall at angle $\theta$ and bounces at angle $\theta$ - is the collision elastic? The source answers 'not necessarily: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence for any smooth-sphere collision regardless of $e$'. That is WRONG for $e < 1$. Correct physics: for a smooth wall the tangential component $v_t$ is unchanged and the normal component becomes $e v_n$. The rebound angle from the normal:

$\tan\theta' = v_t/(e v_n) = (\tan\theta)/e > \tan\theta$ for $e < 1$ - the ball leaves MORE GRAZING, not at the mirror angle. Equal angles then imply $e = 1$ exactly (smooth wall, no spin). With friction (rough wall or spinning ball) the tangential impulse also changes $v_t$ and equal angles no longer pin down $e$ - only then is 'not necessarily' fair.

cards.title: Trap 11 (source C9, corrected): equal bounce angles are NOT free (.
items: Numbers: impact at 45 degrees from the normal at 10 m/s, $e = 0.5$: $v_t = v_n = 7.07$; the normal part becomes $3.54$: rebound angle $\arctan(7.07/3.54) = 63.4$ degrees from the normal - far from 45. Energy: $K_f/K_i = \sin^2 45 + e^2\cos^2 45 = 0.625$ - visibly not elastic.

limit $e = 1$: $\tan\theta' = \tan\theta$ - specular reflection. Limit $e \to 0$: $\theta' \to 90$ degrees - the ball skims the wall (normal motion killed, tangential survives). The formula interpolates physically.

cards.title: Trap 12 (source P5 ambiguity): velocity exchange is 1-D only
items: Source P5: 'two equal-mass balls collide elastically, one at rest; after: (a) the incoming ball stops (d) they move at 90 degrees' with answer (a). Correct only in 1-D. In 2-D the general outcome is the 90-degree separation with the shooter deflected at speed $u\cos\theta_1$ - it stops only in the head-on limit. Safe exam sentence: 'in 1-D the velocities exchange (shooter stops);
in 2-D they separate at 90 degrees and the shooter generally keeps speed $u|\cos\theta_1|$'.

cards.title: Trap 12 (source P5 ambiguity): velocity exchange is 1-D only (cont.
items: Trap 13 (source Q13 under-specification): 'a chain of mass 3 kg is lifted at 2 m/s, find the force' has no unique number without a length scale - the force grows with the hanging length: $F = \lambda x g + \lambda v^2$. Answer with the formula (as source P34c does) and define $x$ and $\lambda = M/L$.
ambiguity traps are scope traps: the statement leaves a free parameter (dimension, length, frame). Name the parameter and answer parametrically - examiners award the method.
trap 12 numbers: equal masses, shooter at $u$, scatter angle 30: shooter speed $0.866u$ (NOT zero) - one number kills the 'always stops' reading.

cards.title: Sign traps and arithmetic traps
items: Sign trap: $e = (v_2-v_1)/(u_1-u_2)$ needs consistent directions; in 2-D project first. Sign trap: the wall formula needs signed velocities; write the axis before numbers. Sign trap: $K_{loss} = K_i - K_f$ comes out negative for superelastic - not an error, a released spring.

Arithmetic trap (documented in SOURCE-AUDIT): in $v_1 = \frac{(m_1-em_2)u_1 + (1+e)m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$ the factor $(1+e)$ multiplies the WHOLE $m_2 u_2$ term. One dropped $\frac{1}{2}$ in $\frac{1}{2}(3)v_2^2$ produced the source's Q18 error ($6/7$ instead of $6/5$ for $v_1^2$). Three-invariant audits (momentum, $e$, energy) catch every such slip.

cards.title: Validity map: when each formula breaks
items: $\mathbf{R} = \sum m_i \mathbf{r}_i/M$: always (definition); continuous bodies need integration. $M\mathbf{a}_{cm} = \mathbf{F}_{ext}$: always in Newtonian mechanics (needs third-law pairs). $\sum \mathbf{p} = $ const: when net external impulse vanishes in that direction - brief collisions OK by approximation; long pushes not. $e = v_{sep}/v_{app}$:

along the line of impact, passive contacts; superelastic allowed with $e > 1$. Master formulas (3.7): 1-D or normal-direction only; fixed masses. $K_{loss} = \frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2(1-e^2)$: same scope; negative means energy gained.

cards.title: Validity map: when each formula breaks (cont.)

Boat/wedge COM laws: zero external impulse in the tracked direction; frictionless supports. 90-degree rule: equal masses, elastic, smooth, target at rest. Bounce ladder: fixed floor, constant $e$.

cards.title: Pre-submission audit (ten points)
items: before using any formula, say its validity sentence out loud. If a condition fails, fall back to first principles: momentum ledger + energy ledger + geometry.

(1) COM: correct reference point and signed masses. (2) Momentum: asserted why net external impulse is zero (in the relevant direction). (3) Collision classified: elastic / inelastic / sticking, correct $e$. (4) $e$ applied along the line of impact only. (5) Two-stage problems: momentum first, energy second (order locked). (6) Rocket: $\ln(m_0/m_f)$, not $m_0 - m_f$; $v_e$ relative. (7) 2-D:

cards.title: Pre-submission audit (ten points) (cont.)
items: decomposed along and across the line of impact. (8) Energy loss: $\mu$ and $u_{rel}$, not raw masses. (9) Units consistent; $g = 9.8$ or 10 as the problem states. (10) Every sub-part answered; signs of final velocities stated as directions.

Time plan for a 3-question collision section: 2 min triage, 3 min per 1-D problem, 5 min for 2-D or two-stage, 2 min audit. COM problems die by definition; collision problems die by momentum + $e$; flux problems die by $\dot m \Delta v$.

$\mathbf{R} = \frac{1}{M}\sum m_i \mathbf{r}_i$ and $M\mathbf{a}_{cm} = \mathbf{F}_{ext}$ (4.1) - the definition and the only equation of motion for a system. $\mathbf{J} = \Delta\mathbf{p} = \int \mathbf{F} dt$ (4.2) - impulse equals momentum change. $\sum\mathbf{p}_{before} = \sum\mathbf{p}_{after}$ when $\sum\mathbf{F}_{ext} = 0$ (4.3) - conservation, component-wise.

cards.title: The boxed ledger: six formulas that run the chapter (cont.)
items: $e = \dfrac{v_{sep}}{v_{app}} = \dfrac{v_2 - v_1}{u_1 - u_2}$ (4.4) - restitution along the line of impact. $K_{loss} = \frac{1}{2}\mu(u_1-u_2)^2(1-e^2)$ (4.5) - the energy price of any 1-D collision. $\Delta v = v_e \ln\frac{m_0}{m_f}$ (4.6) - the rocket. Plus the two workhorses:
the ledger is deliberately short: everything else in the chapter is a derived special case or a bookkeeping protocol. If a problem does not reduce to one of these plus geometry, the triage was wrong.

cards.title: Limits checklist (each formula, one limit)
items: (4.1): $n = 1$ gives $\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{r}_1$. (4.2): constant force gives $J = F\Delta t$. (4.3): switch off external force and $v_{cm}$ freezes. (4.4): $e = 0$ sticks, $e = 1$ elastic. (4.5): $e = 1$ gives zero loss; $e = 0$ gives $\frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2$. (4.6): $m_f = m_0$ gives $\Delta v = 0$; $m_0/m_f = e$ gives $\Delta v = v_e$ (63% of the mass is propellant).

Which formula when: mass distribution -> (4.1) or negative mass. Force and time -> (4.2). Collision without external force -> (4.3) + (4.4). Given $e$ and velocities -> energy lost from (4.5). Rocket -> (4.6). Pendulum -> (4.3) then energy. Chain/jet/belt -> $\dot m \Delta v$ flux. Boat/wedge -> fixed-COM displacements. Bounce heights -> $e = \sqrt{h_2/h_1}$.

cards.title: Rebuild-the-formula drills (60 seconds each)
items: (a) Derive $K_{loss} = \frac{1}{2}\mu u_{rel}^2(1-e^2)$ from $K = \frac{1}{2}Mv_{cm}^2 + \frac{1}{2}\mu v_{rel}^2$ (CM-09). cards.title: Rebuild-the-formula drills (60 seconds each) (cont.)
items: Each derivation is one algebra chain plus one stated assumption: (a) momentum + $e$; (b) momentum in $dt$, constant $v_e$; (c) momentum + energy + equal masses; (d) superposition of a full body and a negative-mass plug. If you cannot rebuild one in a minute, re-read that sheet's first card.

title: The falling chain: the scale reads THREE times the landed weight
subtitle: Three-times-weight derivation; corrected OL1/D7.10 bookkeeping; variants; problem set.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. OL1 / D7.10; independently checked
takeaway: Falling chain: scale reads three times the landed weight, ending at 3mg; momentum flux plus weight, no exceptions.

cards.title: The falling chain: the scale reads THREE times the landed weight
items: Setup: a uniform chain of mass $m$, length $L$, linear density $\lambda = m/L$ is released onto a scale (either suspended with its lower end just touching the pan, or lifted as a strand and dropped - the two readings agree, see below). Let $x$ be the length that has LANDED (equal to the distance the chain has fallen). The airborne part moves at $v = \sqrt{2gx}$;

mass arrives at rate $\dot m = \lambda v = \lambda\sqrt{2gx}$; the impact force stopping it is $\dot m v = \lambda v^2 = 2\lambda g x$. The scale also carries the landed weight $\lambda x g$. Total: $F = \lambda x g + 2\lambda g x = 3\lambda x g$ - THREE times the weight already on the pan.

cards.title: Falling chain: scale reads THREE times landed weight (cont.)
items: At the instant the last link lands ($x = L$): $F = 3\lambda L g = 3mg$ - the famous three-times-weight reading. Limits: as $x \to 0$, $F \to 0$ (nothing on the pan); the reading climbs linearly with $x$; the peak is exactly at the completion of the landing.

If instead the chain is dropped from a height $h$ ABOVE the pan in a heap (all links fall together), the reading is a single impulse $J = m\sqrt{2gh}$ over the collision time, not the smooth $3mg$ ramp - geometry decides the history, but the flux law $\dot m v$ never changes.

cards.title: Falling chain: scale reads THREE times landed weight (cont.)
items: Correction to the source (recorded in SOURCE-AUDIT): source OL1 and its D7.10 brief compute $F = \lambda(L+x)g$ with $x$ = length still falling and conclude $2mg$ at the end. That bookkeeping pairs the wrong speed with the wrong length (it sets $v = \sqrt{2g\ell}$ with $\ell$ the AIRBORNE length;

in fact the airborne speed is $\sqrt{2g\times\text{descent}} = \sqrt{2g x_{landed}}$). The source README itself advertises the 'three-times-weight result' - the corrected derivation delivers exactly that. Use $F = 3\lambda x g$ with $x$ = landed length = descent.

cards.title: Falling chain: scale reads THREE times landed weight (cont.)
items: the factor 3 = 1 (weight) + 2 (flux): the flux term $\lambda v^2 = 2\lambda g x$ is TWICE the landed weight $\lambda x g$ at every instant because $v^2 = 2gx$ while weight grows as $gx$. Momentum flux is not a small correction here - it dominates.

units: $3\lambda x g = 3$(kg/m)(m)(m/s$^2$) = N. Derive the flux term independently: momentum of the falling part changes as links are arrested; force = rate of momentum destruction $= (\lambda v) v$.

title: The falling chain: the scale reads THREE times the landed weight (cont.)
subtitle: Three-times-weight derivation; corrected OL1/D7.10 bookkeeping; variants; problem set.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. OL1 / D7.10; independently checked
takeaway: Falling chain: scale reads three times the landed weight, ending at 3mg; momentum flux plus weight, no exceptions.

cards.title: Variant geometry: the strand lifted from a pile and released
items: Variant B (source OL1's words 'piled on a scale, one end lifted and released'): lift a strand (the whole chain) and release. The falling portion descends with $v^2 = 2g y$ where $y$ is the DESCENT (not the airborne length!). Landing rate $\lambda v$, impact $\lambda v^2 = 2\lambda g y$; landed weight $\lambda y g$ (the landed length equals $y$ when the strand's lower end started at the pan).
Then $F = 3\lambda y g$ again - identical formula with $y$ = descent = landed length. The 3mg endpoint is robust across these geometries.

cards.title: Variant geometry: the strand lifted from a pile and released (cont.)
items: If instead the whole chain is a heap at rest and simply released from height $H$ above the pan (all links airborne at once): the reading is an IMPULSE spike $J = m\sqrt{2gH}$ averaged over the short collision, not a smooth ramp - different problem, same momentum bookkeeping. The exam rule: identify what is falling, at what speed, landing at what rate - then $F = $ landed weight $+ \dot m v$.
dimensional and limit checks on variant B: $F(y) = 3\lambda y g$ grows from 0 to 3mg; quasi-static limit: at vanishing fall speed the flux term dies and the pan reads just the landed weight.

cards.title: Why the naive answer is 2mg (and why it fails)
items: The tempting wrong bookkeeping: airborne length $\ell$, speed $\sqrt{2g\ell}$ (WRONG pairing: speed follows the FALL DISTANCE, not the remaining airborne length), landed $= L - \ell$, giving $F = \lambda(L-\ell)g + 2\lambda g \ell = \lambda(L+\ell)g \to 2mg$. The error:

for a strand whose leading end has descended $y$, the airborne portion has length $L - y$ (started as one full strand) and speed $\sqrt{2gy}$; substituting $\ell = L - y$ into $\sqrt{2g\ell}$ mis-states the speed whenever $y \ne \ell$. Only at ONE instant ($y = \ell = L/2$) do the two agree - which is why the wrong answer survives spot checks at mid-fall.

cards.title: Why the naive answer is 2mg (and why it fails) (cont.)
items: Sanity probe that exposes it: at $y = L/2$ both give $F = 1.5 mg$ (wrong: $\lambda(L + L/2)g = 1.5 mg$; right: $3\lambda(L/2)g = 1.5 mg$); at $y = L$: wrong $2mg$ vs right $3mg$. The ENDPOINT distinguishes them; the 3mg endpoint is the published classic.

the invariant rule: $F = W_{landed} + \dot m v$ with $\dot m = \lambda v$ and $v$ the ACTUAL landing speed measured from the fall distance. One diagram with labelled speeds prevents the pairing error.
the same 3mg endpoint appears in the equivalent 'chain poured onto a pan at free-fall speed' limit and in the Irodov-style textbook solutions - consistent across treatments.

cards.title: Chain-flux problem set
items: (a) Chain 0.5 kg/m falling onto a pan; reading when 0.4 m has landed (g = 10): $F = 3(0.5)(0.4)(10) = 6$ N. (b) At completion ($L = 2$ m, $m = 1$ kg): $F = 3(1)(10) = 30$ N. (c) Same chain held with the end just on the pan and released - same formula. (d) Compare: the same chain RESTING on the pan reads $mg = 10$ N; the falling version peaks at 3x.

(e) Sand falling at constant rate at constant speed (CM-16) reads $W + \dot m v$; the chain adds the $v^2 = 2gx$ growth. (f) The chain LIFTED at constant speed (CM-18) reads $\lambda x g + \lambda v^2$ with $v$ = lift speed (constant) - the weight term grows, the flux term is constant; the falling chain has BOTH growing.

cards.title: Chain-flux problem set (cont.)
items: drill (a): $3\lambda x g = 3 \times 0.5 \times 0.4 \times 10 = 6$ N; landed weight 2 N; flux 4 N $= 2\lambda g x$ - the 1:2 split.

Setup: projectile $m_1$ at speed $u$ hits target $m_2$ at rest; elastic; smooth; deflects at lab angle $\theta_1$ with target recoil $\theta_2$. Three regimes. (1) $m_1 < m_2$: the projectile can scatter BACKWARD; $\theta_1$ ranges over the full $(0, 180)$ degrees - e.g. a neutron off a lead nucleus bounces anywhere. (2) $m_1 = m_2$: $\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90$ degrees exactly (CM-12); $\theta_1$ itself spans $(0, 90)$.

cards.title: Scattering limits: what mass ratios do to the exit angles (cont.)
items: (3) $m_1 > m_2$: the projectile is FORCED FORWARD: $\theta_1$ is capped at $\theta_{max} = \arcsin(m_2/m_1)$ (the circle-locus picture of CM-15: $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{v}_{cm} + \mathbf{v}'_1$ is the sum of a fixed vector and a vector of fixed length; the extreme direction is tangent to that circle). A bowling ball cannot bounce back off a marble - at best it scatters by $\arcsin(m_2/m_1)$.

The lab target angle: $\tan\theta_2 = \dfrac{\sin\theta_{cm}}{\cos\theta_{cm} + m_1/m_2}$ where $\theta_{cm}$ is the CM-frame scattering angle of the projectile (source OL2's final formula - correct as printed). Consequences: $\theta_2 = (180 - \theta_{cm})/2$ when $m_1 = m_2$; $\theta_2 \leqslant 90$ degrees always;

cards.title: Scattering limits: what mass ratios do to the exit angles (cont.)
items: in the extreme-mass limits $\theta_2 \to \theta_{cm}$ (heavy target) or $\theta_2 \to 0$ (light target).

Correction to the source (recorded in SOURCE-AUDIT): source OL2 lists '$\theta_{max} = \arcsin(m_2/m_1)$ if $m_1 < m_2$' and 180/90 otherwise. The $\arcsin$ cap applies when the PROJECTILE IS HEAVIER ($m_1 > m_2$); for $m_1 < m_2$ there is no cap at all ($\theta_1$ can reach 180). The intermediate values ($\theta_{max} = 180$ for $m_1 < m_2$; 90 for equality; $\arcsin(m_2/m_1)$ for $m_1 > m_2$) are the corrected table.

title: Scattering limits: what mass ratios do to the exit angles
subtitle: Corrected scattering-limit table; circle-locus geometry; tan(theta2) formula; drills.
takeaway: Lab angle: tan(theta) = sin(Theta)/(cos(Theta) + m1/m2); heavy projectiles cannot exceed arcsin(m2/m1).

cards.title: Scattering limits: what mass ratios do to the exit angles (cont.)
items: the cap is the tangency of the momentum triangle: $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{v}_{cm} + \mathbf{v}'_1$ with $v_{cm} = \frac{m_1}{m_1+m_2}u$ and $v'_1 = \frac{m_2}{m_1+m_2}u$ (CM speeds). The direction of $\mathbf{v}_1$ rotates as the impact parameter varies; $\theta_1$ extremises when $\mathbf{v}_1$ is tangent to the circle: $\sin\theta_{max} = v'_1/v_{cm} = m_2/m_1$ - exactly the condition $m_2 \leqslant m_1$.

limit $m_2 \to m_1$: $\arcsin(1) = 90$ degrees - the 90-degree theorem's boundary. $m_2 \ll m_1$: $\theta_{max} \to 0$: heavy projectile never deflects. $m_2 > m_1$: the tangent construction fails and every $\theta_1 \in (0, 180)$ is reachable.

cards.title: Worked: the maximum-deflection geometry
items: Head-on elastic against a target of mass $m_2 < m_1$ would send $v_1 = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}u > 0$ straight through; the MAXIMUM deflection instead occurs at a glancing impact parameter. Method: (1) compute $v_{cm} = \frac{m_1 u}{m_1+m_2}$, CM speeds $u'_1 = \frac{m_2 u}{m_1+m_2}$, $u'_2 = -\frac{m_1 u}{m_1+m_2}$;

(2) elastic CM reversal rotates the relative velocity but preserves each CM speed; (3) $\mathbf{v}_1 = \mathbf{v}_{cm} + \mathbf{v}'_1$ traces the circle radius $u'_1$ centred at $v_{cm}$; (4) the deflection angle is extremal at tangency: $\sin\theta_{max} = u'_1/v_{cm} = m_2/m_1$; (5) the speed at the tangent point: $v_1 = \sqrt{v_{cm}^2 - u_1'^2} = u\frac{\sqrt{m_1^2 - m_2^2}}{m_1+m_2}$.

cards.title: Worked: the maximum-deflection geometry (cont.)
items: Numbers: $m_1 = 2$, $m_2 = 1$, $u = 6$: $v_{cm} = 4$, $u'_1 = 2$; $\sin\theta_{max} = 0.5$: $\theta_{max} = 30$ degrees; $v_1 = \sqrt{16 - 4} = 3.46$ m/s at that extremum; target flies off at $\theta_2$ with speed set by the momentum triangle: $\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_{cm} + \mathbf{v}'_2$ with $|v'_2| = 4$;
compute $\theta_{cm}$ from $\tan\theta_1 = \frac{u'_1 \sin\theta_{cm}}{v_{cm} + u'_1\cos\theta_{cm}}$ (projectile lab angle from the CM decomposition).

cards.title: Worked: the maximum-deflection geometry (cont.)
items: verify the 2:1 numbers via the master formulas at a special impact parameter: head-on $\theta = 0$: $v_1 = (2-1)6/3 = 2$, $v_2 = 2(2)(6)/3 = 8$ - circle check: $v_1 = |v_{cm} - u'_1| = 2$; opposite extreme $v_1 = v_{cm} + u'_1 = 6$ (zero deflection) - the circle intersects the forward axis at 2 and 6; the deflection extremum is the tangent at 30 degrees - consistent.

cards.title: Olympiad problem patterns (source OL2 family)
items: 'Find the maximum angle the projectile can be deflected through' -> $\arcsin(m_2/m_1)$ if heavier, else 180 degrees. 'Find $\theta_2$ in terms of $\theta_{cm}$ and masses' -> the $\tan\theta_2$ formula. 'Show $\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90$ for equal masses' -> CM-12's dot product. 'Find the impact parameter for maximum deflection' -> the tangent geometry: $b = (R_1+R_2)\sin\phi$ with $\phi$ set by the tangent construction - derive per problem from the circle.

cards.title: Olympiad problem patterns (source OL2 family) (cont.)

A ball collides with a fixed surface over a short time $\tau$ with a contact force $F(t)$ that spikes far above every other force in the problem. The impulse approximation: ignore gravity/friction during $\tau$ and write $J = \int_0^\tau F dt = \Delta p$; then resume the smooth motion with the new velocity. Source OL3: 0.1 kg ball at 10 m/s bouncing elastically off a floor:

cards.title: When a finite force acts for a blink: the impulse approximation (co.
items: $J = 2mv = 2$ N s (reversal doubles the momentum swing). If instead the contact force peaks at 1000 N over 2 ms: $J_{contact} = 2$ N s exactly - the pulse alone reverses the ball; gravity's impulse over 2 ms is $mg\tau = 0.002$ N s, a 0.1% correction. The approximation is honest: state the scale separation.

Source OL3's second half: same ball rolling at 10 m/s stopped by friction $\mu = 0.5$ in 2 s: impulse $= \mu mg t = 0.5(1)(2) = 1$ N s - NOT equal to the collision impulse 2 N s because the ball's momentum change is only 1 N s (stops, no reversal). The comparison teaches impulse bookkeeping: $J = |\Delta p|$ for whatever the actual velocity change is; reversal costs 2mv, stopping costs mv.

cards.title: When a finite force acts for a blink: the impulse approximation (co.
items: Force-pulse problem types: (i) given $F(t)$ shape (rectangular, triangular, half-sine): integrate the shape. (ii) given average force and duration: $\bar F \tau = \Delta p$. (iii) given $F_{max}$ and shape: $J = F_{max} \tau / k$ with shape factor $k$ (triangle: $J = \frac{1}{2}F_{max}\tau$; half-sine: $J = \frac{2}{\pi}F_{max}\tau$). (iv) given a spring stop: use energy instead; the max force is $kx_{max}$ at max compression.

the approximation is a singular perturbation: over $\tau \to 0$ the impulse $\int F dt$ stays finite while the displacement $\int v dt$ vanishes - positions freeze, velocities jump. This is the mathematical licence for 'collision at a point'.

cards.title: When a finite force acts for a blink: the impulse approximation (co.
items: self-check on OL3 numbers: $J = 2$ N s vs gravity impulse $0.002$ N s - ratio 1000; state the ratio in an exam answer to justify the approximation. If the pulse lasted 0.2 s instead of 2 ms, gravity's $0.2$ N s would matter - check $mg\tau \ll J$ every time.

constraint impulses at BOTH supports enter the momentum ledger - solve with momentum + the rigid-body rotation constraint (advanced; olympiad training).

takeaway: Impulse approximation: F_impulse dt far exceeds other impulses; gravity is a rounding error in a bat-ball collision.

cards.title: Multi-body impulses and constraint impulses (cont.)
items: Ball hitting a wedge of finite mass: not a wall - use the two-body master formulas along the line of impact (wedge momentum changes; wedge slides). Ball hitting a SPRING: no impulse approximation - solve the SHM matching. The choice of tool is set by the contact duration and the partner's mobility.
consistency: for a finite-mass partner, $J$ on the ball and $J$ on the partner are equal/opposite (third law) - if your two $J$s differ, the solution is wrong.

cards.title: Impulse drills
items: (a) 0.2 kg ball at 8 m/s hits a wall and rebounds at 6: $J = 0.2(14) = 2.8$ N s. (b) Same ball dropped 1.25 m on concrete ($e = 0.5$): impact $v = 5$; rebound 2.5; $J = 0.2(7.5) = 1.5$ N s. (c) Triangular pulse peaking at 400 N over 6 ms: $J = \frac{1}{2}(400)(0.006) = 1.2$ N s. (d) Ball 0.15 kg stopped by a 30 N average force: $J = 0.15(25) = 3.75$; $\tau = 3.75/30 = 0.125$ s.

Trap: using $J = F_{max}\tau$ for a non-rectangular pulse (overestimates by the shape factor). Trap: forgetting the sign reversal cost $2mv$ vs $mv$. Trap: comparing impulses of contacts with different durations without normalising to $\Delta p$.

cards.title: Impulse drills (cont.)
items: drill (c) shape factor check: half-sine of same peak and width would give $J = \frac{2}{\pi}(400)(0.006) = 1.53$ N s - shape matters by tens of percent.

When the force history is unknown, bound it: $J = \Delta p$ is exact; if the stop distance $d$ is known, the average force satisfies $\bar F = \frac{mv^2}{2d}$ (work-energy) - often more useful than the time-average. Example: 0.15 kg ball at 25 m/s stopped in 0.5 m: $\bar F = \frac{mv^2}{2d} = \frac{0.15 \times 625}{2 \times 0.5} = 93.75$ N.

cards.title: Impulse bounds and force estimates without the pulse shape (cont.)
items: Compare with a 30 N average force giving $\tau = 0.125$ s (the earlier drill) - two different averages of the same impulse.

Shape factors: rectangular pulse $J = F_{max}\tau$; triangular $J = \frac{1}{2}F_{max}\tau$; half-sine $J = \frac{2}{\pi}F_{max}\tau$. If a problem quotes only $F_{max}$, the answer for $J$ must carry the shape assumption explicitly.
consistency: the time-average and space-average forms must both reproduce $J = \Delta p$; if your two estimates of $J$ disagree, the assumed shape is inconsistent with the given numbers.

title: Ball on a vertically moving platform: the energy-pump machine
subtitle: Bounce map v' = (1+e)u - ev; lift frame solution; energy pump; drills.
takeaway: Bounce map v_new = (1+e)u - e v; a rising platform pumps energy; in the lift frame it is an ordinary bounce.

cards.title: Ball on a vertically moving platform: the energy-pump machine
items: A platform moves vertically with prescribed speed law $u(t)$; a ball is released above it with restitution $e$ at every contact. One-bounce law (CM-21): up-positive, ball velocity $v$ (negative if falling), platform $u$: $v_{after} = (1+e)u - e v_{before}$. If the platform RISES at $u$ into a ball falling at speed $w$: $v_{after} = (1+e)u + e w$ upward.
The platform can therefore pump the ball to arbitrary heights if it keeps rising at the right moments - this is the 'bouncing ball on a piston' machine.

cards.title: Ball on a vertically moving platform: the energy-pump machine (c.
items: Two regimes. (1) Moving lift at constant speed $U$ (upward): ball dropped in a lift rising at $U$: relative problem in the lift frame: ball speed relative $w$, bounce $ew$; the LAB speed after n bounces grows like a geometric ladder that converges if $e < 1$ to a fixed relative speed where the per-bounce gain $(1+e)U$ balances the per-bounce loss $(1-e)w$: $w_* = \frac{(1+e)U}{1-e}$ in the platform frame.

cards.title: Ball on a vertically moving platform: the energy-pump machine (c.
items: (2) Oscillating platform: resonance when the platform arrives upward exactly as the ball arrives - phase locking; POGO/springboard questions use this.

The classic exam configuration (source OL6, with the pure bounce ladder in source OL4): platform initially at rest accelerates up at constant $a$ while a ball bounces with $e$; find the speed after n bounces or the conditions for the ball to keep bouncing. Method: time between bounces $t_n = 2v_n/g_{rel}$ (with platform acceleration folded into an effective $g$ in the platform frame:

cards.title: Ball on a vertically moving platform: the energy-pump machine (c.
items: $g_{eff} = g + a$ for a platform accelerating UP); apply the bounce law at each contact; the sequence can be summed if $e$ is constant.

the machine is the olympiad playground for relative-speed restitution: every contact is a one-line map $v \mapsto (1+e)u - ev$; the composition of maps is where the richness lives. Energy is NOT conserved - the platform's motor does work through the normal force.

cards.title: Ball on a vertically moving platform: the energy-pump machine (c.
items: static limit: platform at rest ($u = 0$): $v_{after} = -e v_{before}$; ball on a steadily rising platform in equilibrium: the fixed point of the map $v' = (1+e)U - ev$ is $v = U$ - the ball just rides at the platform speed, bouncing at zero relative speed - physical.

Ball dropped from rest relative to the lift floor; lift rises at $U$ (constant). In the lift frame: ball falls with speed growing as $gt$; hits at relative speed $w = \sqrt{2gh}$ (h = drop height in the frame); rebounds at $ew$; rises to $e^2 h$; the cycle repeats with $h \to e^2 h$. In the LAB frame each rebound speed is $U + ew$ (from the map with $v_{before} = U - w$):

cards.title: Worked: ball dropped in a lift rising at constant speed U (cont.)
items: $v_{after} = (1+e)U - e(U - w) = U + e w$; relative speed up $= ew$ - consistent with the frame picture.

Steady state: the relative speed after bounce is $e^n w_0 \to 0$ for $e < 1$; the ball settles to riding at $U$ with tiny hops. For $e = 1$: relative speed preserved; the ball keeps bouncing forever at the same relative amplitude, drifting with the lift. Energy in the lab: KE plus PE grows as the lift rises - the motor pays.

relative-frame audit: every bounce in the lift frame is the textbook fixed-floor bounce with $e$; the lab is a pure velocity shift. If a lab-frame calculation disagrees with the frame-shifted answer, the sign convention broke.

cards.title: Platform-machine drills
items: (a) Ball dropped 2 m in a lift rising at 3 m/s, $e = 0.5$, $g = 10$: relative impact speed $w = \sqrt{40} = 6.32$; lab after $= 3 + 0.5(6.32) = 6.16$ m/s up. (b) Platform rising at 2 m/s meets ball falling at 4 m/s (lab), $e = 0.8$: $v_{after} = (1.8)(2) + 0.8(4) = 6.8$ m/s up. (c) Driven steady relative speed in a lift rising at $U = 1$ with $e = 0.5$:
$w_* = \frac{1.5}{0.5} = 3$ m/s (for periodic kicks; a pure drop decays to 0 instead).

Trap: applying the map with lab speeds and forgetting the $(1+e)u$ platform term. Trap: using $g$ instead of $g + a$ in the platform-accelerating case. Trap: assuming energy conservation anywhere in this machine.

cards.title: Platform-machine drills (cont.)
items: drill (b) energy sanity: ball KE grew from $\frac{1}{2}m(16)$ to $\frac{1}{2}m(46)$ - platform motor did work; momentum is NOT conserved (platform is external).

Platform $u(t) = u_0\cos\omega t$; ball released above. Each bounce maps $v \mapsto (1+e)u(t_n) - e v$ at contact times $t_n$. Phase locking: if the ball always meets the platform rising near its maximum $u_0$, the gain per bounce is maximal $(1+e)u_0 + e w$ - the POGO condition. If the flight time $2v/g$ equals an integer number of platform periods, the phase repeats and the bounce ladder is a clean geometric series.

items: Numbers: platform $u = 2\cos(2t)$, ball dropped in phase with the peak: first bounce with $w = 5$, $e = 0.5$: in phase: $(1+e)u + ew = 3 + 2.5 = 5.5$ m/s up. Out of phase (platform at $-u_0$): $v_{after} = -3 + 2.5 = -0.5$ - barely bounces.

cards.title: Chain over a smooth peg: the full solution, including the moment it.
items: Setup (source OL7): a uniform chain of mass $m$, length $L$ hangs over a frictionless peg with length $x$ on one side and $L - x$ on the other, released from rest at some $x_0 > L/2$. (1) Acceleration: the unbalanced weight is $\lambda x g - \lambda(L-x)g = \lambda g(2x - L)$ on total mass $m = \lambda L$: $a = \dfrac{g(2x-L)}{L}$. At $x = L/2$:

$a = 0$ (unstable equilibrium); at $x = L$: $a = g$ - the whole chain is in FREE FALL at the end (source OL7's key line). (2) Speed: $v\,dv = a\,dx$ gives $v^2 = \frac{2g}{L}\left[(x - \frac{L}{2})^2 - (x_0 - \frac{L}{2})^2\right]$; released from rest exactly at $L/2$ plus a nudge, $v^2 = \frac{2g}{L}(x - \frac{L}{2})^2$.

cards.title: Chain over a smooth peg: the full solution, including the moment it.
items: (3) Peg force - the part everyone botches. The peg feels the weight $mg$ MINUS the momentum-flux term of the strand going slack:
writing the chain's downward momentum $p = \lambda v(2x - L)$ gives $\frac{dp}{dt} = 2\lambda[v^2 + (x-\frac{L}{2})a] =
4\lambda v^2$ (consistent substitution), so $F_{peg} = mg - 4\lambda v^2 = mg\left[1 - \dfrac{2(2x-L)^2}{L^2}\right]$ for the nudge-from-centre release.

cards.title: Chain over a smooth peg: the full solution, including the moment it.
items: The peg force DECREASES as the chain accelerates - it does not spike. Contact is lost when $F = 0$: $(2x-L)^2 = L^2/2$, i.e. $x = \frac{L}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \approx 0.854L$; beyond that the chain flies off the peg (formal $F < 0$ is unphysical for a peg that can only push).

Why the folklore '3mg at the end' is wrong for THIS problem: the classic 3mg belongs to the chain LANDED ON A SCALE (OLY-01: weight + landing flux both grow). The sliding peg problem has the opposite structure: the moving chain goes slack against the peg as $a \to g$; the end-of-motion peg force tends to zero, not to $3mg$. The two chain problems bracket the flux law:

title: Chain over a smooth peg: the full solution, including the moment it lets go
subtitle: Peg solution: a = g(2x-L)/L, v^2(x), F_peg = mg[1-2(2x-L)^2/L^2], contact loss at 0.854L; corrected folklore.
takeaway: Chain over a peg: a = g(2x-L)/L, v^2 = (2g/L)(x - L/2)^2; peg force falls to zero at x = 0.854L - the chain lets go.

cards.title: Chain over a smooth peg: the full solution, including the moment it.
items: onto a pan the flux ADDS to the reading ($\lambda v^2$ with $v$ of landing); over a peg the flux of the TURNING strand is fed by the chain's own weight and the peg sheds load.

the momentum-ledger method is the only safe route for moving-chain problems: write $p(t)$ for the whole chain, differentiate, equate to $W - F$. Strand-by-strand tension bookkeeping easily double-counts the flux. The source's ODE method ($v\,dv = a\,dx$) and the momentum method are the two halves of the complete solution.

cards.title: Chain over a smooth peg: the full solution, including the moment it.
items: limits: $x = L/2$: $F = mg$, $v = 0$ (static). $x \to L$: $a \to g$, $F \to -mg$ (already detached). Energy: $\frac{1}{2}m v^2 = $ PE drop: PE $= -\frac{\lambda g}{2}[x^2 + (L-x)^2]$; drop from $L/2$ to $x$: $\Delta PE = -\lambda g(x - \frac{L}{2})^2$; KE $= \lambda g(x-\frac{L}{2})^2 = \frac{1}{2}m v^2$ with $v^2 = \frac{2g}{L}(x-\frac{L}{2})^2$ - exactly consistent.

the detachment fraction is geometry-independent of $m$, $g$: $x_{detach}/L = \frac{1}{2}(1 + 1/\sqrt{2}) = 0.854$ exactly - a pure number worth quoting in an exam answer as the 'loss of contact' condition.

Peg-problem toolkit and drills (cont.)

for a chain FLOWING over a peg into motion on both sides (no slack): $F = W + 2\lambda v^2$ (flux ADDS) - e.g. the fold-release family of OLY-08. Slack vs pulling downstream is the single most important qualitative judgement in chain problems.

cards.title: Peg-problem toolkit and drills (cont.)
items: Tension at a point of the moving chain: cut the chain; $T = $ (weight of the part beyond the cut) + (flux of momentum across the cut) + (mass beyond x acceleration). For the peg problem: the strand tension just below the peg is $T = \lambda g \ell + \lambda \ell a$ for a hanging strand of length $\ell$ accelerating at $a$ (the strand's own weight plus its acceleration). At the nudge-release with $\ell = L - x$: $T = \lambda g(L-x) + \lambda(L-x)a$.

cards.title: Tension along the moving chain (cont.)
items: Drill: $L = 1$, $x = 0.7$ (nudge release): $a = 2g(0.2) = 4$; $\ell = 0.3$: $T = 0.3(10) + 0.3(4) = 4.2$ N for $\lambda = 1$ kg/m. The peg force is the sum of the two strand tensions at the peg (which equals $mg - 4\lambda v^2$ as derived) - the two bookkeepings agree.
at $x = L/2$ (equilibrium, $v = 0$, $a = 0$): $T = \lambda g L/2 = mg/2$ each side; the peg holds $mg$ total.

cards.title: Why rockets have stages: drop the dead metal
items: A rocket stage burns its propellant then throws away its empty tank and engine (structural mass). The next stage starts from a lighter vehicle. Model (source OL8): total mass $M$, payload $M_p$; structural coefficient $\epsilon = m_{structure}/m_{initial\,of\,stage}$; exhaust speed $v_e$. A stage with initial mass $m_i$ burning until $m_f$ gives $\Delta v = v_e \ln(m_i/m_f)$;
at burnout the empty structure $\epsilon m_i$ is DISCARDED before the next burn. That discard is what breaks the telescoping of the logs - and it is the entire benefit of staging.

cards.title: Why rockets have stages: drop the dead metal (cont.)
items: Mass timeline discipline: draw $M_0 \to$ (burn 1) $\to m_1 \to$ (discard structure) $\to m_2 \to$ (burn 2) $\to m_f$. Then $\Delta v = v_e[\ln(M_0/m_1) + \ln(m_2/m_f)]$ with $m_2 = m_1 - m_{structure,1}$. Forget the discard and the two logs telescope to the useless $v_e \ln(M_0/m_f)$; discard BEFORE burnout and you threw away propellant mass you had not used.

Numbers (source P30 with consistent bookkeeping; the source's printed staging mixes two split conventions - recorded in SOURCE-AUDIT): $M_0 = 1000$ kg, two stages of 400 kg propellant + 50 kg structure each, payload $M_p = 100$ kg: stage 1 burns to 600 kg, discard 50, stage 2 starts at 550, burns to 150:

title: Why rockets have stages: drop the dead metal
subtitle: Staging ledger; mass timeline; corrected P30 numbers (5.43 vs 4.83 km/s); drills.
source: Source: centre-of-mass-momentum/Centre-of-mass-momentum.md sec. OL8 / P30; independently checked
takeaway: Staging: with zero structure any split gives v_e ln(M/M_p); the real gain is dropping spent tanks.

cards.title: Why rockets have stages: drop the dead metal (cont.)
items: $\Delta v = v_e[\ln(1000/600) + \ln(550/150)] = v_e(0.511 + 1.299) = 1.81 v_e = 5.43$ km/s at $v_e = 3$ km/s. Single-stage with the same total propellant and structure (100 kg kept to the end): $\Delta v = 3\ln(1000/200) = 3\ln 5 = 4.83$ km/s. Staging wins by about 12% with identical hardware.

cards.title: Why rockets have stages: drop the dead metal (cont.)
items: the rocket equation punishes carried mass logarithmically; dropping empty tanks deepens the mass ratio per burn. With zero structural mass any split gives the same $\Delta v = v_e \ln(M/M_p)$ - structure is the ONLY reason to stage.

limits: $\epsilon \to 0$: staged = unstaged; $M_p \to M$: $\Delta v \to 0$; more stages (fixed hardware) always increase $\Delta v$ until the interstage hardware itself dominates. Timeline closes: $400+400+50+50+100 = 1000$ kg.

cards.title: Optimal split and the multistage ladder
items: For two identical stages (equal $\epsilon$, equal $v_e$): the total $\Delta v = v_e[\ln(M/m_1) + \ln(m_2/m_f)]$ under the mass-timeline constraint; the optimisation (Jensen on the logs) equalises the two stage $\Delta v$s for maximum total at fixed hardware. With $n$ stages and fixed total structure mass, more stages keep helping until interstage hardware eats the gain - real rockets stop at $n = 2$ or 3.

cards.title: Optimal split and the multistage ladder (cont.)
items: With gravity: $\Delta v_{net} = \sum v_e \ln(m_i/m_f) - g t_{burn}$; staging also keeps acceleration high in thin air, cutting gravity loss - the engineering trade-off beyond the textbook ledger. The same ledger governs 'drop ballast mid-journey' puzzles and two-block spring mass-shedding (CM-14).
for identical stages the optimal equal-split principle is a one-line AM-GM argument: $\ln a + \ln b = \ln(ab)$ is maximal at fixed $a + b$ when $a = b$ - equal logs, equal $\Delta v$.

title: Why rockets have stages: drop the dead metal (cont.)
subtitle: Staging ledger; mass timeline; corrected P30 numbers (5.43 vs 4.83 km/s); drills.

takeaway: Staging: with zero structure any split gives v_e ln(M/M_p); the real gain is dropping spent tanks.

cards.title: Optimal split and the multistage ladder (cont.)
items: single vs staged audit in ratio form: $\frac{\Delta v_{staged}}{\Delta v_{single}} = \frac{\ln(1000/600)+\ln(550/150)}{\ln 5} = \frac{1.810}{1.609} = 1.125$ - exactly 12.5% more $\Delta v$.

(a) Single stage: $M = 1000$, propellant 800, structure 100, payload 100: $\Delta v = v_e \ln 5 = 1.61 v_e$. (b) Two stages (the worked case): $1.81 v_e$ - beats (a) by $0.20 v_e$. (c) Three stages of 266.7 propellant + 33.3 structure each, payload 100: the timeline is $1000 \to 733.3 \to 700 \to 433.3 \to 400 \to 133.3$ (burn, discard, burn, discard, burn;

cards.title: Staging drills (cont.)
items: the last structure rides along). Then $\Delta v = v_e[\ln(1000/733.3) + \ln(700/433.3) + \ln(400/133.3)]$ $= v_e[0.310 + 0.480 + 1.099] = 1.89 v_e$ - three stages beat two, which beat one: monotone improvement.
