cards.title: Inverse staging: sizing the rocket for a mission
items: Given $\Delta v$ target and $v_e$: required mass ratio $m_0/m_f = e^{\Delta v / v_e}$. Mission $\Delta v = 9$ km/s at $v_e = 3$ km/s: ratio $= e^3 = 20.1$ - the payload + structure must be under 5% of launch mass. With structural coefficient $\epsilon$ per stage, $n$ stages give successively deeper ratios; the practical answer: two stages at $\epsilon = 0.1$ reach ratios around 10-15 - matching real launchers.

Gravity-loss back-of-envelope: at thrust-to-weight 1.3, the gravity loss $\approx g t_{burn}$ quoted from the burn time, not from $\Delta v$ alone; a 9 km/s mission at $a = 2g$ loses roughly half a km/s to gravity in the first minutes.

cards.title: Inverse staging: sizing the rocket for a mission (cont.)
items: reverse the worked case: 5.43 km/s at $v_e = 3$ needs ratio $e^{1.81} = 6.1$; the staged design delivers $1000/150 = 6.67$ - consistent with the timeline (final mass includes the last structure).

A circular jet of area $A$, speed $v$, density $\rho$ strikes a large fixed flat plate and spreads along it (source OL9). Mass rate $\dot m = \rho A v$; the normal momentum is destroyed (the water leaves tangentially): $F = \dot m v = \rho A v^2$. For a plate tilted at angle $\theta$ to the jet axis (normal force only): $F_n = \rho A v^2 \cos\theta$; at angle $\theta$ to the PLATE surface:

title: Jet on a plate: F = rho A v^2, and the moving-plate power game
subtitle: Jet flux law; moving plate P = rho A (v-u)^2 u with u = v/3 optimum; cup factor 2; drills.
takeaway: Jet on a plate: F = rho A v^2 normal component; on a moving plate the relative speed (v - u) does the work.

cards.title: Jet on a plate: F = rho A v^2 & power game (cont.)
items: $F_n = \rho A v^2 \sin\theta$ - read the angle definition from the diagram before multiplying.

Moving plate at speed $u$ in the jet's direction: the relative speed is $v - u$, so $F = \rho A (v-u)^2$ and the power delivered to the plate is $P = Fu = \rho A (v-u)^2 u$. Maximise over $u$: $dP/du = 0$ gives $u = v/3$ (not $v/2$!) with $P_{max} = \frac{4}{27}\rho A v^3$. The turbine designer's law: the jet should be slowed to one third. At $u = 0$ (fixed plate) $P = 0$;
at $u = v$ (plate flees with the jet) $F = 0$ and $P = 0$; the maximum sits between.

cards.title: Jet on a plate: F = rho A v^2 & power game (cont.)
items: If the water does not spread but rebounds elastically (curved cup): the normal momentum REVERSES: $F = 2\dot m v = 2\rho A v^2$ (the cup variant of source OL9) - double the flat-plate force. A Pelton-wheel cup nearly doubles the force of a flat target; the same factor-2 logic as the turn flux in chain problems.

the jet is the cleanest possible flux problem: control volume = the water in contact; momentum in $\rho A v^2$ per second along the normal; momentum out zero (flat) or reversed (cup). If the jet discharges to atmosphere there are no pressure terms - the whole force is momentum flux.

cards.title: Jet on a plate: F = rho A v^2 & power game (cont.)
items: A hose or gun ejecting $\dot m$ at $v_e$ feels recoil $\dot m v_e$ - the rocket thrust (CM-17) in static form. A fire hose of 5 kg/s at 20 m/s: 100 N on the firefighter. A sprinkler cart: thrust = mass rate x relative jet speed; the cart accelerates like a rocket with water as exhaust. The jet-pump / turbine family: same flux law with the right control volume.

cards.title: Recoil as flux; the jet taxonomy (cont.)
items: Water falling on a moving horizontal belt: retarding force $= \dot m(v - u)$ with $u$ the belt speed (CM-16 family). The exam taxonomy: jet on plate $\rho A v^2$; cup $2\rho A v^2$; moving plate $\rho A(v-u)^2$; belt pickup $\dot m v$; rocket $\dot m v_e$. One law, five costumes.

recoil audit: 0.5 kg/s at 15 m/s: 7.5 N; pump power $= \frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2 = 56$ W = the jet's KE rate; the plate absorbs $Fu$ on top of that in the belt-split sense - consistent with CM-16's factor-2 bookkeeping.

title: Jet on a plate: F = rho A v^2, and the moving-plate power game (cont.)
subtitle: Jet flux law; moving plate P = rho A (v-u)^2 u with u = v/3 optimum; cup factor 2; drills.
takeaway: Jet on a plate: F = rho A v^2 normal component; on a moving plate the relative speed (v - u) does the work.

cards.title: Jet drills
items: (a) Jet $A = 4$ cm$^2$, $v = 10$ m/s on a flat plate: $F = 40$ N. (b) Same on a plate at 45 degrees to the jet axis (normal force): $F_n = 28.3$ N. (c) Moving plate at 4 m/s: $F = 1000(4\times10^{-4})(36) = 14.4$ N; $P = 57.6$ W. (d) Cup reversal: double (a): 80 N. (e) Optimal turbine speed for a 20 m/s jet: $u = 6.67$ m/s; $P_{max} = \frac{4}{27}(1000)(4\times10^{-4})(8000) = 474$ W.

cards.title: Jet drills (cont.)
items: Trap: using $v$ instead of $v - u$ for moving plates. Trap: angle measured from the wrong reference. Trap: missing the factor 2 for rebound cups. Trap: equating $P_{max}$ with the jet's KE rate $\frac{1}{2}\rho A v^3$ - the best useful power is only $\frac{8}{27}$ of the jet's KE rate, about 30%.

cards.title: Efficiency curve of a turbine stage
items: Useful power $P = \rho A (v-u)^2 u$ rises from 0 at $u = 0$, peaks at $u = v/3$ with $P_{max} = \frac{4}{27}\rho A v^3$, falls to 0 at $u = v$. Efficiency $\eta = P/(\frac{1}{2}\rho A v^3)$: at the peak $\eta = 8/27 = 30$%. The Pelton cup shifts the force constant up by the factor 2 in the flux; the $u = v/3$ optimum is unchanged.

cards.title: Efficiency curve of a turbine stage (cont.)
items: curve sanity: $P(v/4) = \rho A (3v/4)^2 (v/4) = \frac{9}{64}\rho A v^3 = 0.141$ vs peak $0.148$ - near-flat top; real impulse turbines cluster $u/v$ near 1/2 with cups.

Clean statement (source OL10, whose 'COM \L/4' phrasing is ambiguous - recorded in SOURCE-AUDIT; this is the standardised version): a uniform chain of mass $m$, length $L$ is folded at its MIDPOINT and laid on a smooth horizontal table with the fold just past the smooth edge, so BOTH halves hang together. Released from rest.

title: Folded chain released over a smooth edge: v = y sqrt(2g/L)
subtitle: Folded chain: v = y sqrt(2g/L), departure sqrt(gL/2); ambiguity guard for OL10; drills.
takeaway: Folded chain off a smooth edge: v = y sqrt(2g/L) with y the fold depth; leaves the table at sqrt(gL/2).

cards.title: Folded chain released over a smooth edge: v = y sqrt(2g/L) (cont.)
items: Let $y$ = the descent of the fold = the length of EACH hanging strand (total hanging length $2y$). Speed: energy with hanging mass $2\lambda y$ and COM at depth $y/2$: PE loss $= 2\lambda y \cdot g \cdot \frac{y}{2} = \lambda g y^2$; KE $= \frac{1}{2}\lambda L v^2$ (the WHOLE chain moves at speed $v$ - the fold is a rigid corner). So $\frac{1}{2}\lambda L v^2 = \lambda g y^2$:
$v = y\sqrt{\dfrac{2g}{L}}$ - speed linear in descent, NOT $\sqrt{2gy}$ as for a free particle.

cards.title: Folded chain released over a smooth edge: v = y sqrt(2g/L) (cont.)
items: Departure: the chain leaves the table when the fold has descended $y = L/2$ (both strands fully hanging): $v_{dep} = \frac{L}{2}\sqrt{\frac{2g}{L}} = \sqrt{\frac{gL}{2}}$. After that the chain falls free with its departure speed. The law $v \propto y$ means constant acceleration:
$a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \sqrt{\frac{2g}{L}} v = \frac{2g}{L}y$ - the fold accelerates in proportion to its own depth (a linear instability, kin to the chain-over-peg ODE of OLY-05).

cards.title: Folded chain released over a smooth edge: v = y sqrt(2g/L) (cont.)
items: Force on the edge (flux bonus): the doubled strand turns over the edge at rate $2\lambda v$; the edge feels hanging weight plus a turn-flux term of the $2\lambda v^2$ family with the doubled density. The exam answer quotes the energy line and $v_{dep} = \sqrt{gL/2}$; the force bookkeeping is a fair exercise on the momentum ledger of OLY-05.

the fold constrains BOTH halves to move together - one velocity, one degree of freedom. That is why the whole chain's KE uses $L$ while the PE uses only the hanging $2y$: the energy equation is unusually clean and $v = y\sqrt{2g/L}$ is exact.

cards.title: Folded chain released over a smooth edge: v = y sqrt(2g/L) (cont.)
items: limits: $y = 0$: $v = 0$; $y = L/2$: $v = \sqrt{gL/2}$; $g \to 0$: $v \to 0$. Units: $y\sqrt{g/L} = $ m $\times$ s$^{-1}$ = m/s. Compare free fall through $y$: $\sqrt{2gy}$ vs fold $y\sqrt{2g/L}$ - at $y = L/2$: free $\sqrt{gL}$ vs fold $\sqrt{gL/2}$: the fold is SLOWER (half the chain is still on the table).

Variant A: fold NOT at the midpoint (strands of unequal length): the shorter strand runs out first; beyond that it is a single-hanging-strand problem - piecewise solve. Variant B: fold on the table with the fold-point LIFTED then released (the 'COM + L/4' reading of source OL10): the answer depends on the exact initial shape - define the geometry in the diagram before solving.

title: Folded chain released over a smooth edge: v = y sqrt(2g/L) (cont.)
subtitle: Folded chain: v = y sqrt(2g/L), departure sqrt(gL/2); ambiguity guard for OL10; drills.
takeaway: Folded chain off a smooth edge: v = y sqrt(2g/L) with y the fold depth; leaves the table at sqrt(gL/2).

cards.title: Variant geometries and the ambiguity guard (cont.)
items: Variant C: rough table: friction on the table-lying part retards; energy loses the friction-work term. Variant D: the chain is pushed initially: from $\frac{1}{2}\lambda L v^2 = \frac{1}{2}\lambda L v_0^2 + \lambda g y^2$: $v^2 = v_0^2 + \frac{2g y^2}{L}$.
variant D limit: $y = 0$ gives $v = v_0$; at $y = L/2$, $v_0 = 0$ recovers $v = \sqrt{gL/2}$.

(a) $L = 2$ m, $g = 10$: $v = y\sqrt{10} = 3.16y$; at $y = 0.4$ m: $v = 1.26$ m/s; departure at $y = 1$ m: $v = 3.16$ m/s ($= \sqrt{gL/2} = \sqrt{10}$). (b) Unequal fold (strands $L/4$ and $3L/4$ hanging, i.e. NOT a doubled fold): different problem - use the peg-style ODE of OLY-05. (c) Compare departure speeds: fold $\sqrt{gL/2}$;

cards.title: Fold drills (cont.)
items: single strand sliding off a peg to $x = L$: $v = \sqrt{gL/2}$ as well - the two ODEs are first cousins.

Trap: treating the fold as two independent strands (they are kinematically tied - ONE $v$). Trap: using $\sqrt{2gy}$ (free fall) for the fold. Trap: forgetting the on-table part of the chain in the KE sum.

cards.title: Fold as a variable-mass Atwood
items: The fold's equation $a = \frac{2g}{L}y$ is a variable-mass Atwood: the driving weight $2\lambda y g$ acts on the accelerating mass $\lambda L$: $a = \frac{2\lambda y g}{\lambda L} = \frac{2gy}{L}$ - the same result as the energy route. The Atwood perspective shows WHY the fold accelerates: the hanging weight grows while the inertia stays fixed.

Compare: classic Atwood (two fixed masses): $a = g\frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ = const; fold: $a \propto y$ = exponential runaway; peg: $a = g(2x-L)/L$ = linear. Three ODE shapes in one family: constant, linear, linear-in-y - each with its own $v^2(x)$.

cards.title: Fold as a variable-mass Atwood (cont.)
items: Atwood limit of the fold: freeze $y$ at $y_0$ (clamp): $a = 2gy_0/L$ constant - reduces to a fixed-mass Atwood with effective masses $2\lambda y_0$; the clamp force appears - consistent bookkeeping.

The demand: conservation of momentum must hold in ALL inertial frames. If $p = m v$ with invariant $m$, a Lorentz transformation of a simple collision gives different momenta in different frames - the law fails. The unique form (up to an overall constant) that transforms correctly is $\mathbf{p} = \gamma m \mathbf{v}$ with $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$.

title: Why momentum must be gamma m v (source OL5)
subtitle: p = gamma m v from frame-independence; scope fence for classical mechanics; preview of PART 28.
takeaway: p = gamma m v is the unique momentum that conservation keeps covariant; mass stays invariant.

cards.title: Why momentum must be gamma m v (source OL5) (cont.)
items: Derivation sketch (the standard two-frame elastic collision argument): write $p = m f(v)$; demand that a collision viewed in the lab and in a boosted frame both conserve $p$; the functional equation forces $f = \gamma$.

Consequences previewed here (full treatment is relativistic dynamics): (1) $\gamma \approx 1 + \frac{v^2}{2c^2}$ at low speed, so $p \approx mv$ up to tiny corrections - Newtonian mechanics is the $v \ll c$ shadow. (2) Force is $dp/dt$ not $ma$: $F = \gamma^3 m a$ along the motion - a constant force cannot accelerate a mass to $c$.

cards.title: Why momentum must be gamma m v (source OL5) (cont.)
items: (3) Relativistic KE $= (\gamma - 1)mc^2 \to \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ as $v \to 0$; the full series is $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{3}{8}\frac{mv^4}{c^2} + \ldots$ (4) The 'mass increase' $m \to \gamma m$ is a historical way of writing the same formula - the modern view keeps $m$ invariant and changes the momentum law (source OL5's Significance).

For classical olympiad/JEE mechanics: the exam-relevant point is the scope statement - all our conservation laws assume $v \ll c$; when speeds approach $c$, momentum conservation still holds but with $p = \gamma mv$ and $e$-type restitution becomes frame-dependent and subtle. Keep this sheet as the fence around the classical playground.

cards.title: Why momentum must be gamma m v (source OL5) (cont.)
items: the deep principle: conservation laws are statements about symmetry (translation invariance of space and time). The relativistic momentum is what survives when both symmetries act together - the classical $mv$ is the low-speed limit of the correct object, not a definition.
low-speed limit $v/c = 0.1$: $\gamma = 1.005$: a 0.5% correction to $p$ - invisible in every chapter problem. $v = 0.9c$: $\gamma = 2.29$: more than double $mv$ - classical mechanics gone.

cards.title: The two-frame argument in one paragraph (cont.)
items: Take an elastic collision between identical particles, symmetric in the CM. Boost along the collision axis. In Newtonian physics the velocity addition $u' = u - V$ preserves momentum conservation. In relativity, velocity addition is $u' = \frac{u - V}{1 - uV/c^2}$;
requiring conservation in both frames with $p = m f(u)$ gives a functional equation for $f$ whose unique regular solution is $f(u) = \gamma u$ (up to constant $m$).

title: Why momentum must be gamma m v (source OL5) (cont.)
subtitle: p = gamma m v from frame-independence; scope fence for classical mechanics; preview of PART 28.
takeaway: p = gamma m v is the unique momentum that conservation keeps covariant; mass stays invariant.

cards.title: The two-frame argument in one paragraph (cont.)
items: Rest mass is invariant: every observer agrees on $m$; they disagree on $p$ and $E$. Energy-momentum forms a four-vector $(E/c, \mathbf{p})$; $E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2$ unifies the ledger: massless particles have $p = E/c$ (photons); massive at rest have $E = mc^2$.

relativistic collisions still use the same triage: choose the frame (CM is best), conserve the four-momentum, transform back. The 90-degree rule of CM-12 becomes 'the angle opens ABOVE 90 for relativistic equal-mass collisions in the lab' - a classic modern-physics exam twist.

cards.title: The two-frame argument in one paragraph (cont.)
items: energy-momentum checks: photon $m = 0$: $E = pc$; electron at rest: $p = 0$, $E = mc^2$; Newtonian ledger recovered for $E - mc^2 \ll mc^2$: $E \approx mc^2 + \frac{p^2}{2m}$.

(1) Momentum conservation is the more fundamental law; $F = ma$ is its low-speed shadow. (2) The classical chapter's formulas (3.7, 4.5, 4.6) are all $v \ll c$ statements - state the assumption when speeds are given as 'large'. (3) The rocket equation assumes non-relativistic exhaust; relativistic rockets integrate $\Delta p = v_e dm$ with $\gamma$ folded in.

cards.title: What to carry back into classical mechanics (cont.)
items: (4) Restitution ($e$) has no clean relativistic definition for extended bodies - modern physics avoids it.

Exam context: this sheet is the olympiad extension layer (the source lists it as OL5, a PART-28 preview). For JEE the one-line takeaway: $p = \gamma mv$ reduces to $mv$ at low speed and momentum is conserved in all frames - the syllabus does not require the derivations.
limit drill: $\gamma - 1 \approx v^2/2c^2$ at $v = 0.01c$: $5\times10^{-5}$ - the classical error is one part in 20,000.

cards.title: Gamma drills
items: (a) $v = 0.5c$: $\gamma = 1.155$; (b) $v = 0.8c$: $\gamma = 1.667$; (c) $v = 0.99c$: $\gamma = 7.09$; (d) KE at 0.8c $= (\gamma-1)mc^2 = 0.667 mc^2$ - twice the Newtonian $\frac{1}{2}m(0.64c^2) = 0.32 mc^2$. (e) A proton at rest has $E = 938$ MeV; at $\gamma = 4$: total 3.75 GeV, KE 2.81 GeV.
Momentum at 0.8c for 1 kg: $p = \gamma m v = 1.667(1)(2.4\times10^8) = 4\times10^8$ kg m/s vs Newtonian $2.4\times10^8$ - a 67% understatement. The classical ledger fails visibly above $0.5c$.

title: Why momentum must be gamma m v (source OL5) (cont.)
subtitle: p = gamma m v from frame-independence; scope fence for classical mechanics; preview of PART 28.
takeaway: p = gamma m v is the unique momentum that conservation keeps covariant; mass stays invariant.

cards.title: Gamma drills (cont.)
items: A cart of mass $M_0$ (empty) rolls at $v_0$ on a smooth floor under a hopper that drops sand at rate $\dot m$ (kg/s). Collecting mode (source family CM-16/Q22): horizontal momentum is conserved (dropped sand has none): $M(t)v(t) = M_0 v_0$ with $M(t) = M_0 + \dot m t$: $v(t) = \dfrac{M_0 v_0}{M_0 + \dot m t}$. The retarding force at any instant:

cards.title: Cart under a hopper: the full variable-mass ledger
items: $F = \dot m v$ (the sand must be dragged from 0 to $v$). Power drained from the cart's KE: exactly $\frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2$ - half becomes the sand's KE, half becomes pickup heat (CM-16's factor-2).

Leaking mode: a cart of mass $M$ at $v$ leaks sand vertically at rate $\dot m$: the dropped sand carries horizontal momentum $\dot m v$ away per second, so $\frac{d}{dt}(M v) = \dot m v$; with $\frac{dM}{dt} = -\dot m$ this gives $M \dot v = 0$: $v$ CONSTANT. The classic surprise: a leaking cart does not slow down; only loading slows it.

cards.title: Cart under a hopper: the full variable-mass ledger (cont.)
items: Engine mode: a cart with engine force $F$ collecting sand: $\frac{d}{dt}[(M_0 + \dot m t)v] = F$; solve the linear ODE. With constant power $P$ instead: $\frac{d}{dt}[\frac{1}{2}M v^2] = P - \frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2$ (the pickup tax). The hopper family is the rocket equation with the sign of $\dot m$ flipped and no exhaust speed - same ledger, one diagram.

cards.title: Cart under a hopper: the full variable-mass ledger (cont.)
items: these three modes (load, leak, thrust) exhaust the first-order variable-mass list for exam mechanics; the momentum ledger in $dt$ is the single method. The surprise results (leaking keeps $v$; loading burns half the delivered power as heat) are examiner favourites because they punish intuition.

collecting numbers: $M_0 = 20$ kg at 5 m/s, $\dot m = 0.1$ kg/s, at $t = 100$ s: $v = 100/30 = 3.33$ m/s; KE: 250 J to $\frac{1}{2}(30)(11.1) = 166.6$ J; the 83.4 J lost is pickup heat, matching the differential identity $\frac{1}{2}\dot m v^2 = -\frac{d}{dt}KE$ (verified in CM-16).

title: Cart under a hopper: the full variable-mass ledger
subtitle: Load/leak/thrust modes; sprinkler and mixed flows; drills with the surprise results.
takeaway: Hopper cart: loading slows (F = m_dot v), leaking does not; the d(Mv)/dt ledger solves all three modes.

cards.title: Sprinkler cart and jet recoil (the same ledger)
items: Sprinkler: cart + water tank ejects water at $\dot m$ with speed $v_e$ relative to the cart (usually backward): thrust $\dot m v_e$; the cart is a rocket with water propellant: $\Delta v = v_e \ln(M_0/M_f)$ if $\dot m$ runs to dry. Fire-extinguisher recoil: treat the spray as exhaust. A cart under a leaky bucket with a pump: combine loading and thrust terms in one $dt$ equation.

cards.title: Sprinkler cart and jet recoil (the same ledger) (cont.)
items: Mixed problem: cart collects rain at $\dot m_1$ while ejecting at $\dot m_2$ with relative speed $v_e$: the systematic form is $M\dot v = F_{ext} + \dot m_{in}(u_{in} - v) + \dot m_{out}(u_{out} - v)$ with all velocities lab-frame; the CM-16 sign discipline sets each term.
sprinkler limit: no water: $\Delta v = 0$; no external force with ejecta: momentum of cart + ejecta conserved exactly.

cards.title: Hopper drills
items: (a) Cart 30 kg at 6 m/s collects 2 kg of dropped sand: $v = 180/32 = 5.625$ m/s. (b) Cart 30 kg at 6 m/s LEAKS 2 kg vertically: $v = 6$ m/s unchanged. (c) Cart 30 kg at rest ejects 5 kg backward at 4 m/s relative to the cart: ejected lab speed $= v - 4$; momentum $0 = 25v + 5(v-4) = 30v - 20$: $v = 0.67$ m/s.
(d) Engine force 60 N while loading at 0.2 kg/s (cart 30 kg at 6 m/s initially): $(30 + 0.2t)v = 180 + 60t$; at $t = 10$: $32v = 780$: $v = 24.4$ m/s.

cards.title: Hopper drills (cont.)
items: Trap: forgetting the $\dot m v$ retarding term when loading. Trap: assuming leaking slows the cart. Trap: using $\Delta v = v_e \ln(\cdot)$ for a collecting cart (that formula is for ejecting mass).

title: Cart under a hopper: the full variable-mass ledger (cont.)
subtitle: Load/leak/thrust modes; sprinkler and mixed flows; drills with the surprise results.
takeaway: Hopper cart: loading slows (F = m_dot v), leaking does not; the d(Mv)/dt ledger solves all three modes.

cards.title: Explicit solutions of the loading-engine ODE
items: $\frac{d}{dt}[(M_0 + \dot m t)v] = F$ integrates directly: $(M_0 + \dot m t)v = M_0 v_0 + F t$: $v(t) = \dfrac{M_0 v_0 + F t}{M_0 + \dot m t}$. Long-time limit: $v \to F/\dot m$ (the engine can only hold that asymptote while dragging new mass). With $F = 0$ it reduces to the pure-loading decay $M_0 v_0/(M_0 + \dot m t)$; with $\dot m = 0$ it is uniform acceleration.

cards.title: Explicit solutions of the loading-engine ODE (cont.)
items: differentiate the closed form at $t = 0$: $\dot v = [F M_0 - \dot m M_0 v_0]/M_0^2 = (200 - 10)/100 = 1.9$ m/s$^2$; the ODE $M\dot v = F - \dot m v = 20 - 1 = 19$ gives $\dot v = 1.9$ - the two agree.

cards.title: When momentum needs calculus: the three integration patterns
items: Pattern 1 - VARIABLE FORCE with time: $J = \int F(t) dt = \Delta p$; if $F$ depends on $v$ (drag), write $m\frac{dv}{dt} = F(v)$ and separate: $\frac{m\,dv}{F(v)} = dt$; integrate. Pattern 2 - VARIABLE FORCE with position: $F = F(x)$; use work-energy $\int F dx = \Delta K$ instead (or $v\,dv = a\,dx$). Pattern 3 - VARIABLE MASS:
the $dt$ ledger of CM-16/OLY-10: $\frac{d}{dt}(Mv) = F_{ext} + \dot m_{in}u_{in} - \dot m_{out}u_{out}$; solve the linear ODE.

cards.title: When momentum needs calculus: the three integration patterns (co.
items: Worked (chain ODE, source OL7 method): $a = g(2x-L)/L$ with $v = dx/dt$: $v\,dv = a\,dx$ integrates to $v^2(x)$; then $dt = dx/v(x)$ integrates to $t(x)$ - the two-integration pattern of every chain problem. Worked (drag): $m\dot v = -bv$: $v = v_0 e^{-bt/m}$ - exponential relaxation; distance $= \frac{mv_0}{b}(1 - e^{-bt/m})$;
the body never stops in finite time - a favourite limit question.

subtitle: Three integration patterns; separable toolkit; phase-line sketch; drills with the drag and chain ODEs.

takeaway: Three integration patterns: J = int F dt for F(t), work-energy for F(x), the M-v ledger for variable mass.

cards.title: When momentum needs calculus: the three integration patterns (co.
items: Worked (rocket with gravity): $m\dot v = -v_e \dot m - mg$ with $m = m_0 - \dot m t$: $\Delta v = v_e \ln(m_0/m_f) - g t_b$ - the $dt$ ledger with a prescribed $m(t)$. The integration pattern is identical to the hopper engine mode (OLY-10) with sign changes.

momentum conservation is a first-order statement about $p$; as soon as the force law or the mass law is nonlinear, the exam problem is really a differential equation. The triage: (i) is $F$ given as $t$, $x$, or $v$? (ii) is mass constant? (iii) choose $J = \int F dt$ or work-energy accordingly.

cards.title: When momentum needs calculus: the three integration patterns (co.
items: drag limit checks: $b \to 0$: $v \to v_0$; $t \to \infty$: $v \to 0$ with finite distance; large $b$: stops almost immediately. Chain ODE check: $v^2 = \frac{2g}{L}(x - \frac{L}{2})^2$ differentiated back gives $a = \frac{2g}{L}(x-\frac{L}{2})$ - matches Newton.

$m v \frac{dv}{dx} = F(x)$: energy in disguise. $m \frac{dv}{dt} = F(v)$: time-separable. $\frac{d}{dt}(M(t)v) = F(t)$: integrating factor $1/M(t)$. $\frac{d}{dt}(Mv) = \dot m u$: variable mass. Recognising WHICH of the four forms a problem takes is the whole exam skill; each has a one-line solution template.

cards.title: The separable-equation toolkit for mechanics
items: Phase-line view (olympiad flavour): for $a = a(x)$ the fixed points are $a = 0$ (equilibrium; stable if $da/dx < 0$); the chain over the peg has unstable equilibrium at $x = L/2$; the fold has $a \propto y$ (no fixed point except 0, unstable). Sketching $a$ vs $x$ before integrating prevents sign errors in $v^2(x)$.

cards.title: The separable-equation toolkit for mechanics (cont.)
items: numerical fallback: if the ODE has no closed form (e.g. $v^2$ drag plus thrust), Euler-step in a table - method marks come from the SETUP $m\dot v = \ldots$, and a one-step estimate often answers 'show that the speed exceeds...' questions.
toolkit sanity: every template above is just $F = dp/dt$ rearranged; if two templates disagree on a shared problem, the bookkeeping of $M(t)$ vs $m$ is wrong.

items: (a) $m = 2$ kg, $F = 6t$ N: $\Delta p = \int_0^2 6t\,dt = 12$ N s; $\Delta v = 6$ m/s. (b) $F = -kx$ from $x = 0$ to $A$: work-energy: $\Delta K = -\frac{1}{2}kA^2$ (spring stop: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$). (c) Drag $bv$ with $b = 0.4$, $m = 1$, $v_0 = 10$: after 2 s: $v = 10 e^{-0.8} = 4.49$ m/s. (d) Chain $L = 1$, $g = 10$, nudge release:

cards.title: Integration drills (cont.)
items: Trap: using $J = F_{avg}t$ when $F$ is not constant - integrate instead. Trap: mixing $F(x)$ problems into $\int F dt$ (wrong variable). Trap: losing the $\frac{1}{2}$ in $v\,dv = a\,dx$ integration ($v^2/2$, not $v^2$).

cards.title: Integration drills (cont.)
items: drill (d) via energy: $v(x) = \sqrt{20}(x-0.5)$ comes from $v^2 = 20(x-0.5)^2$ (OLY-05); $t = \int dx/v$ = the second integration of Pattern 1.

Near an unstable equilibrium, $a \approx \lambda_1 (x - x_*)$ with $\lambda_1 > 0$ gives $x - x_* \propto e^{\sqrt{\lambda_1} t}$ - the linearised escape law. Peg: $x_* = L/2$, $a = \frac{2g}{L}(x - \frac{L}{2})$: departure rate $\sqrt{2g/L}$; a 1% displacement grows by $e$ in time $\sqrt{L/2g}$. For $L = 1$ m: 0.15 s per e-fold.

cards.title: Linearise around the fixed point: the exponential departure (cont.)
items: Stable side: if $a = -\omega^2(x-x_*)$, the linearised solution is SHM at $\omega$ - the same local analysis classifies every chain/pendulum equilibrium before solving the full ODE.

the fold's $a = \frac{2g}{L}y$ is the same linear form with $y_* = 0$: pure exponential from the start; the peg's full solution $v = \sqrt{2g/L}(x - L/2)$ is the EXACT finite-amplitude version of the linearised escape - they coincide because the ODE is exactly linear in $(x - L/2)$.
